body: BABAR SATTAR, J.- This consolidated judgment will decide the above-titled reference as well as the references listed in Annexure-A.

2. While a host of questions have been formulated by the applicants in the mentioned references (a complete list of which is appended as Annex A), the elemental question in all these references, whether filed by the Customs Department or private citizens, is whether the finding by a Forensic Science Laboratory Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 3 (“FSL”) that the chassis number of a vehicle is tampered is dispositive of the fact that such vehicle is smuggled in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, 1969 (“Customs Act”)? The affiliated question is one of consequences: where the chassis number of a vehicle is found to be tampered, can such vehicle be released to the owner under any circumstances or must such vehicle always be confiscated and its title vested in the State in terms of Section 182 of the Customs Act?

3. The answers to these primary questions are then contingent on other questions of law involving interpretation of provisions of the Customs Act. The first issue that the Court must attend to is the scope of this Court's reference jurisdiction in terms of Section 196 of the Customs Act and whether in exercise of such jurisdiction this Court can interpret provisions of the Customs Act that impinge on whether or not a vehicle that forms the subject-matter of the reference is to be released to its purported owner or confiscated by the State? The answer to the question of what constitutes smuggling for purposes of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, inviting the penalties prescribed under Section 156 of the Customs Act, requires interpretation of Section 187A of the Customs Act to decipher the legislative intent behind such provision introduced through the Finance Act, 2025. The second foundational question that arises is whether penalties under clauses (9), (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act can be imposed in relation to a vehicle without first rendering a finding of wrongdoing against the owner of a vehicle held liable for the offence of smuggling. In other words, for purposes of clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act is the penalty for wrongdoing to be imposed on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 4 property in rem, or is the penalty to be imposed in personam after rendering a finding that the purported owner of the property is liable for wrongdoing? In this context, the question of how property rights and the right to due process and fair trial guaranteed by Articles 9, 23, 24 and 10A of the Constitution are to be balanced against public interest and the legitimate interest of the State in preventing and deterring smuggling in terms of provisions of the Customs Act requires consideration. This discussion would then necessarily require an appreciation of how the principle of proportionality is to be applied where an order for confiscation of property is to be made and whether such confiscatory order qualifies the test of being the least restrictive means to realize a legitimate State objective that has the effect of fettering the right to property guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution.

4. In terms of determining the question of wrongdoing and liability, there is need to interpret how burden of proof is to be discharged for purposes of Section 156(1) read with Sections 187 and 211 of the Customs Act, how the requirement to discharge the burden of proof continues to shift during the adjudicatory proceedings, and the implication of application of the best evidence rule to such proceedings. What also requires determination is how case property is to be administered during the adjudicatory proceedings, starting from the detention of a vehicle through other stages starting from its detention and seizure through confiscation and thereafter till the adjudicatory proceedings attain finality. This requires appreciation of how the notions of safe custody and safe transmission of case property are to be understood and applied while interpreting Sections Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 5 168, 169 and 182 of the Customs Act? In this context, the Court would also need to delineate the scope of Customs General Orders (“CGOs”) issued in terms of Section 223 of the Customs Act and whether such CGOs can regulate exercise of authority under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act or expand the scope of authority vested pursuant to Section 182 of the Customs Act. What also requires interpretation is the scope of Section 169(4) of the Customs Act and how the principles of safe custody of case property, while a matter is sub-judice, is to be squared with Section 201 read with Section 169(4) of the Customs Act, to understand and interpret the circumstances in which case property can be sold off or put to use by the State while the property remains the subject-matter of adjudicatory proceedings and its title remains vested in a private individual.

5. This Court is seeking to undertake a holistic appraisal of how provisions of the Customs Act are to be read and understood keeping in view the constitutional guarantees underscoring the right of citizens to fair trial, due process and property rights, which have sometimes escaped the attention of adjudicatory authorities, as evident from conflicting case law on the question of confiscation of vehicles found or deemed to be tampered. We will therefore start with considering the scope of our reference jurisdiction followed by an appraisal of the relevant constitutional principles and how they impinge on the various provisions of the Customs Act identified above for purposes of understanding how the process of detaining, seizing and confiscating vehicles deemed to be smuggled, while upholding the rights of vehicle owners to fair trial and due process and to uphold their right to property while balancing the same against Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 6 the legitimate State interest of preventing and deterring smuggling in Pakistan. Such analysis will be followed by interpretation of the various provisions of the Customs Act to explain how a finding of wrongdoing in view of the relevant record and evidence during the adjudicatory proceedings is a prerequisite for imposition of liability in terms of Section 156 of the Customs Act. And how case property is to be preserved and its safe transmission ensured in order for an FSL report re the chassis number or chassis plate of an allegedly tampered vehicle to have evidentiary value, especially where such tampered chassis plate is the primary or sometimes the only basis for the assertion that the vehicle in question is smuggled. The analysis will be undertaken in the larger context of how the relationship between the citizen and the State is to be understood and what affirmative steps the State is required to take in its fiduciary capacity before imposing penalties on citizens, where the effect of such penalty acquires the form of confiscation of the citizen's property. The legal analysis will follow the relevant factual details of individual references, then leading to adjudication of questions framed in relation to such references. The arguments of learned counsel for vehicle owners and the Customs Department have not been summarized separately in order not to elongate this already lengthy judgment, but have been dealt with as part of the legal analysis.

Custom Reference No.12 of 2022 6. A Toyota Land Cruiser (2700 CC), Registration No. BH- 779-ICT, Model 2010, Chassis No. TRJ150-0008697, was intercepted and detained on 08.12.2020, and subsequently seized on 21.12.2020. A Show-Cause Notice was issued to the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 7 owner of the vehicle and through Order-in-Original dated 24.02.2021, the vehicle was ordered to be confiscated on the basis that its chassis number had been tampered with and that the prosecution had established that the vehicle had been brought into the country illegally without payment of duties and taxes. The owner of the vehicle, Raza Khan s/o Altaf Khan, submitted before the Collector that he was a bona fide purchaser of the seized vehicle. He stated that the vehicle had originally been purchased by Muhammad Bilal, resident of Dosali, North Waziristan Agency, under the Amnesty Scheme, 2013, who had deposited duties and taxes amounting to Rs.4,627,661 under Order-in-Original No. 7903 dated 30.03.2013, issued by the Deputy Collector Customs, Kohat. Subsequently, Minallah Jan (CNIC No. 21506-8295775-1) purchased the vehicle, which was registered in his name by MRA Islamabad with Registration No. BH-779. Thereafter, the present owner purchased the seized vehicle from Raza Akram s/o Muhammad Akram, resident of Faisalabad, through Pak Motors and Property Advisor, G.T. Road, Sarai Alamgir. It was further contended that the Customs Department had not verified the particulars of the seized vehicle by scrutinizing the data available with it regarding imports, auctions, or vehicles cleared under the Amnesty Scheme. The vehicle was reflected at Serial No. 351 in the data of vehicles cleared under the Amnesty Scheme, 2013 by Customs at Kohat (MCC Peshawar). It was also asserted that, at the time of clearance of vehicles under the Amnesty Scheme, 2013, no mechanism existed for verifying chassis numbers in order to determine whether they were genuine or had been tampered with or cut and welded. The Tribunal, however, upheld the order of confiscation, observing that the tampered chassis number of Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 8 the vehicle did not tally with the documents produced before MRA Islamabad for the purpose of registration.

Custom Reference No.77/2023 7. A Toyota Aqua, Registration No.ANX-668-ICT, Model 2014 (Chassis No.NHP10-6295729), was intercepted and detained on 12.07.2021. It was seized on 09.08.2021. A Show- Cause Notice dated 26.08.2021 was issued to the owner and by Order-in-Original dated 18.10.2021, the confiscation of the vehicle was ordered on the basis of FSL report dated 15.07.2021, which rendered a finding that the chassis plate of the vehicle was cut and welded. The Customs Appellate Tribunal (“Tribunal”) set-aside the Order-in-Original for having been passed beyond a period of 30 days and thus being in contravention of the requirement of Section 179(3) of the Customs Act. It noted that a second forensic examination ordered by the Collector was not carried out. The owner of the vehicle produced goods declaration as well as tax payment receipts verified by the Customs Appraisement (East), Karachi, by letter dated 29.07.2022. The Tribunal took into account the fact that there was no other vehicle according to the record that had the same chassis number and that there was no proof of smuggling in the matter. The findings were rendered while taking into account the fact that the vehicle was stolen on 29.06.2019 and the vehicle‘s owner registered an FIR in this regard. It was subsequently recovered from Holy Family Hospital in Satellite Town Rawalpindi on 07.12.2020 and the owner was granted superdari under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (“Cr.PC”), by the Judicial Magistrate, Rawalpindi. During the hearing of the reference, this Court had Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 9 directed the Customs Department to provide details with regard to disposal of vehicles confiscated by the Customs Department. The Customs Department relied on ECC decision dated 08.03.2006 and submitted that vehicles with tampered chassis numbers could not be registered by Motor Vehicle Registration Authorities (“MRA”). Such vehicles were to be given to the Government Departments offering the highest price. And any remaining vehicles were to be distributed free of cost to Government owned educational, medical and scientific institutions. The report stated that 122 confiscated vehicles, duly registered with MRA over the last 5 years, were being used by public officials. 404 vehicles that had been confiscated due to tampered chassis numbers had been sold to Government Departments in terms of CGO No.05 of 2018. 555 vehicles with tampered chassis numbers were being used by Field Formations of the Customs Department. 109 vehicles with tampered chassis numbers were being used by Field Formations of the Internal Revenue Service. Such vehicles could not be driven on the roads by private individuals due to security concerns as the authentic identity of such vehicles was not verifiable. However, such vehicles could be used while they were under the control of Government Departments. It was submitted that the total cost of such confiscated vehicles, calculated on the basis of sale of scrap, was Rs.250 million. However, the replacement cost of such vehicles was Rs.9,354 million.

Custom Reference No.100 of 2023 8. A Toyota Land Cruiser Prado, Registration No.JAE-040 (Quetta), Model 2007 (Chassis No.TRJ120-5094993), was intercepted and detained on 17.06.2020. The vehicle was seized Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 10 on 24.06.2020. A Show-Cause Notice was issued to the vehicle owner and by Order-in-Original dated 29.07.2020 the vehicle was ordered to be released to the owner despite an FSL report dated 18.06.2020 establishing that the chassis frame of the vehicle was cut and welded. The Collector (Adjudication) found that the Customs Department had failed to establish that the vehicle was not the one cleared under Amnesty Scheme, 2013. The Tribunal took note of the FSL report that the chassis number of the vehicle was cut and welded. It observed that while the vehicle may have been cleared in the Amnesty Scheme, 2013, but by virtue of SRO No.568(I)/2008 dated 11.06.2008 such scheme excluded vehicles with cut and welded chassis plates. The Tribunal noted the vehicle owner's assertion that the original owner, Sher Muhammad, surrendered the vehicle to avail the benefit of an Amnesty Scheme and paid the requisite duties and taxes. Consequently, a No Objection Certificate was issued for registration of the vehicle after seeking an affidavit that the vehicle was not cut and welded. It also noted that by ECC decision dated 03.03.2006 the Government had decided that vehicles with tampered chassis numbers could not be released and it was therefore the owner and not the Customs Department that was responsible even to the extent that the vehicle was cleared through an Amnesty Scheme. The Tribunal noted that the notion of bonafide purchaser was alien to the Customs Act. In terms of background, an FIR No.143/2016 dated 25.04.2016 was registered against the vehicle owner for offences under Sections 420, 468 and 471 of the Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”). The owner's application under Section 249-A of Cr.PC was dismissed. The vehicle owner then filed Writ Petition No.2364 of 2016 before the Islamabad High Court, which after Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 11 taking into account the Amnesty Scheme details and verifying that duties and taxes had been paid pursuant to such scheme ordered the release of the vehicle on superdari by judgment dated 23.04.2016. The vehicle was then detained, as discussed above, on 17.06.2020. The vehicle owner then filed Writ Petition No.2817 of 2020 before the Islamabad High Court, which by judgment dated 17.11.2020 ordered the release of the vehicle subject to furnishing of surety. The Customs Department filed an appeal against such judgment, but the Supreme Court refused to grant leave by order dated 28.09.2021 in CP No.3462 of 2020. The Customs Department, however, refused to release the vehicle to the owner, despite court orders, during the pendency of adjudicatory proceedings.

Custom Reference No.214 of 2023 9. A Toyota Premio, Registration No.ARQ-007 (Sindh), Model 2004 (Chassis No.ZTT240-0044208), was intercepted and detained on 23.09.2020. The vehicle was seized on 28.09.2020 and Show-Cause Notice dated 03.11.2020 was issued to the owner of the vehicle. The Order-in-Original dated 24.11.2020 ordered the confiscation of the vehicle on the basis of FSL report dated 24.09.2020, which found that the chassis number was grinded and self-punched. The chassis number, as apparent, was ZZT240-0091512, which after chemical treatment was deciphered to be ZZT240-0044208. The Order-in-Original noted the owner's response that the vehicle had been purchased from Raja Riaz Hussain on 05.12.2017 and Rs.900,000/- was paid in consideration through banking channels. The seller disappeared and FIR No.297/19 dated 03.04.2019 was registered against the seller, when the owner realized that the vehicle was tampered as Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 12 a consequence of FSL report dated 10.04.2019. The custody of the vehicle was granted to the owner on superdari after the seller/accused was declared a proclaimed offender. The Orderin-Original was based on the fact that it was not denied that the vehicle was tampered and therefore its confiscation was ordered. The Tribunal by order dated 09.08.2023 set-aside the Order-in- Original on the basis that the forensic examination was carried out without associating the owner with the fact that the vehicle was lawfully registered in the name of the owner who was a bonafide purchaser and the Customs Department possessed no evidence of smuggling of the vehicle. It was also noted that the vehicle had remained in the possession of the Customs Department for a significant period creating doubt about how its chassis number was tempered.

Custom Reference No.05 of 2024 10. A black Toyota Land Cruiser, Registration No.AAH-418 (Punjab), Model 2017 (Chassis No.URJ202-4142902), was detained on 16.08.2023 and seized on 24.08.2023 due to its chassis number being manually punched. A Show-Cause Notice dated 08.09.2023 was issued to the owner of the vehicle. The Order-in-Original dated 08.09.2023 ordered the confiscation of the vehicle on the basis of FSL report dated 07.08.2023, which concluded that the chassis number was manually punched and the vehicle was smuggled in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act. The Tribunal by order dated 21.12.2023 upheld the Order-in-Original while relying on the law laid down by the Peshawar High Court in Sultan Muhammad vs. Collector Customs and another (2015 PTD 570) and the Supreme Court in Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa vs. Sarfraz and others (2020 SCMR 1410) and Ch. Maqbool Ahmed vs. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 13 Customs, Federal Excise and Sales Tax, Appellate Tribunal and 3 others (2009 SCMR 226). The Tribunal also ordered a second forensic examination, which was done and a report was submitted on 08.12.2023, which also concluded that the original chassis numbers had been erased and could not be deciphered due to deep grinding and such report had been rendered after associating the owner with the examination process, and was conducted on the owner's request. The Tribunal concluded that the registration book in itself was not evidence of import in a case where the chassis number was found to be tampered and that the notion of bonafide purchaser was alien to the Customs Act. During the proceedings before this Court, the Customs Department submitted that another vehicle with the same chassis number had been traced by the Customs Department. It was this vehicle that was cleared by the Customs Department on the basis of import documents being used by the confiscated vehicle. It bore Sindh registration number BT-0999 and was originally registered by Sheikh Naseer Ahmed on 21.06.2017. It was then purchased by Pir Syed Saleh Shah Jillani. The registration documents of such vehicle reflected that the vehicle was imported and rendered out of charge on 24.03.2017 and had been imported by Auto Mall. It was on the basis of such import documents that the vehicle was registered by the MRA in Sindh. The applicant in rejoinder submitted that the chassis number of the applicant's vehicle was URJ202-41429O2, and confusion was being caused as the second last number in the chassis number of the applicant's vehicle was the alphabet O and not the digit 0. The applicant was, however, unable to produce any import documents that were different from those on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 14 basis of which the vehicle of Pir Syed Saleh Shah Jillani (registration number BT-0999) was registered in Sindh. Custom Reference No.31 of 2024 11. A Toyota Aqua, Registration No.ADV-989 (ICT), Model- 2015 (Chassis No.NHP10-6372366), was intercepted and detained on 23.02.2022. It was seized on 11.04.2022. A Show- Cause Notice dated 12.05.2022 was issued to the vehicle's owner. The vehicle was confiscated through Order-in-Original dated 30.06.2022 on the basis of FSL report dated 28.03.2022, which concluded that the chassis number was tampered and many of the digits could not be deciphered due to deep metallic filling. The chassis number reflected after treatment was NHP10- X3XXXXX. The contention of the vehicle's owner before the Customs Department was that the vehicle was imported by ARB International after auction in Japan. Customs duty in the amount of Rs.684,020/- was paid at the time of import and the vehicle was registered on 14.02.2019. The vehicle was then stolen, which event was reported in FIR No.363/19 dated 17.08.2019. It was subsequently recovered from Peshawar and was handed to the vehicle's owner on superdari by Judicial Magistrate on 16.11.2019. The Magistrate, while passing such order, had taken into account the fact that the engine and chassis numbers had been defaced, but that the vehicle had been opened and started by the owner using the master key in his possession. The Tribunal set-aside the Order-in-Original and noted that the order had been passed 50 days after the issuance of the Show-Cause Notice and was beyond the limit prescribed in Section 179(3) of the Customs Act. On merits, the Tribunal found that the superdari of the vehicle was handed over to the respondent as Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 15 there was no rival claimant of the vehicle. It also noted that the impugned order relied on a replaceable Vehicle Identification Number (“VIN”) plate on the door of the vehicle and a manipulated chassis plate, which reasoning was beyond the allegations stated in the Show-Cause Notice. In view of the physical state of the vehicle as well as the literature associated with the vehicle, the Tribunal concluded that it was a 2015 model car. The Tribunal found that the FSL report did not establish smuggling, when the vehicle was lawfully registered and the owner had established the onus of lawful import by producing original auction documents issued in Japan alongwith the relevant import documents, which documents had been provided to the Excise & Taxation Office (“ETO”) for purposes of registration. In these circumstances, the owner discharged his burden establishing lawful excuse to possess the vehicle and the Customs Department failed to discharge its onus to establish that the vehicle was smuggled in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act.

Custom Reference No.42 of 2024 12. A Toyota Aqua, Registration No.AES-159-ICT, Model-2013 (Chassis No.NHP10-6155549), was intercepted and detained on 20.07.2023. It was seized on 21.08.2023. A Show-Cause Notice dated 12.10.2023 was issued to the vehicle's owner for failure to produce import documents and stated that the vehicle's record was not found in PRAL database. The Order-in-Original dated 10.11.2023 concluded on the basis of FSL report that the chassis number of the vehicle was cut and welded. The vehicle's owner had contended before the Collector that the vehicle had suffered a major accident, while also providing the import documents reflecting the chassis number of the vehicle. An FIR in relation to Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 16 the accident was registered on 20.03.2019. The vehicle's owner asserted that the right pillar of the vehicle was damaged. The Collector dismissed such explanation on the basis that the FIR was insufficient to establish legal import in case where the chassis plate was cut and welded and took note of the fact that no reporting of the accident and the changes effected to the chassis plate had been reported under Section 33 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965 (“Motor Vehicles Ordinance”), while relying on the law laid down by the Peshawar High Court in Sultan Muhammad. The Tribunal set-aside the Order-in- Original while finding that the owner had discharged the onus of proof by producing an accident report and that the Customs Department had failed to discharge its onus to establish that the vehicle was smuggled.

Custom Reference No.61 of 2024 13. A Toyota Prado Jeep, Registration No.BF-4027 (Sindh), Model 2003 (Chassis No.RZJ120-0009742), was intercepted and detained on 08.01.2023 and was seized on 02.02.2023. A Show- Cause Notice dated 27.02.2023 was issued to the owner. An Order-in-Original dated 08.03.2023 ordered the confiscation of the vehicle on the basis of FSL report dated 09.01.2023, which found that the chassis number was grinded and tampered and while the chassis number, as reflected in the record of the vehicle, was RZJ120-0009742, the chassis number after chemical treatment was found to be RZJ120-0001XX4. The owner submitted before the Collector that the vehicle was imported from Japan in 2005 by Samina Zahid. It was not registered and was purchased by Munir Ahmed in 2013, who then got it registered. The Bill of Entry and Import Permit for the vehicle were verified by the Collectorate of Appraisement, Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 17 Customs House, Karachi, by letter dated 03.10.2013. The vehicle was subsequently purchased by Abdul Ghafoor (the father of Danish Ghafoor) on 15.05.2019. The Order-in-Original noted that chassis numbers of legally imported vehicles were often used to hide the identity of smuggled vehicles and that the import details available in the PRAL database related to some other vehicle. But the vehicle in question had been brought into Pakistan through an unauthorized route and was therefore smuggled. The Tribunal by order dated 29.03.2024 set-aside the Order-in-Original through a split verdict. The Member (Judicial) found that the owner had paid full price for the vehicle and was an innocent third party, who had completed all codal formalities to have the vehicle registered. That there was no record establishing that the chassis number of the vehicle had been allotted to any other vehicle, in support of the assertion of the Customs Department that such chassis number belonged to another legally imported vehicle. And the Customs Department had failed to trace the whereabouts of the imported vehicle, the record of which was available in the PRAL database. The Member (Technical) upheld the Order-in-Original on the basis that the FSL report had determined that the vehicle was tampered, while holding that the concept of bonafide purchaser was alien to the Customs Act. The Referee Member found that the owner had produced import documents, including the goods declaration verified by PRAL database as well as the registration documents of the vehicle, thus shifting the onus on to the Customs Department, which failed to discharge such onus as there was no proof of the assertion that the vehicle was smuggled. The Tribunal also took into account the assertion of the vehicle's Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 18 owner that the engine number of the vehicle was the same as that reflected in the import documents of the vehicle. Custom Reference No.74 of 2024 14. A Toyota Corolla Axio, Registration No.AAD-793 (KP), Model 2007 (Chassis No.NZE141-6056808), was intercepted and detained on 15.09.2023. It was seized on 28.09.2023 and a Show-Cause Notice dated 14.12.2023 was issued to the vehicle's owner. The vehicle was confiscated by Order-in-Original dated 02.01.2024, which order stated that the import documents had not been duly verified and produced by the vehicle's owner. The vehicle's owner submitted before the Customs Department that the vehicle was registered for the first time on 20.11.2007 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and had continued to be used for a period of 16 years before it was seized and subsequently confiscated. The ETO in Jaffarabad did not deny that the import documents were not provided, but stated that the record of the office had been burnt down on 28.12.2007 after riots broke out due to the assassination of Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto. The Tribunal upheld the confiscation order by noting that the import documents had not been provided and the record from the ETO had been burnt down in 2007. It found that the vehicle's owner had failed to discharge onus of proof in terms of Section 187 of the Customs Act while noting that there was no concept of bonafide purchaser under provisions of the Customs Act. During the proceedings before this Court, the applicant/vehicle‘s owner produced the original registration book, which had purportedly also been provided to the Customs Department and the Tribunal during the adjudicatory proceedings. The Customs Department, on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 19 other hand, submitted that the vehicle had already been auctioned.

Custom Reference No.07 of 2025 15. A Toyota Aqua, Registration No.EA-882, Model 2015 (Chassis No.NHP10-2131103), was intercepted and detained on 13.02.2024 and subsequently it was seized. A Show-Cause Notice dated 07.03.2024 was issued to the vehicle's owner and through Order-in-Original dated 29.03.2024 the confiscation of the vehicle was ordered on the basis that its chassis number was tampered and the data being relied on by the owner was in relation to some other vehicle. The Collector held that the owner had failed to produce documents of legal import. In terms of factual background, the vehicle was stolen on 27.07.2018 and the owner registered an FIR No.331/2018 on the same date. The vehicle was recovered by Anti-Car Lifting Cell and its possession was handed over to the vehicle‘s owner on superdari by Additional Sessions Judge by order dated 20.11.2018 and in such order the Additional Sessions Judge noted that the owner had identified the vehicle on the basis of the physical state of the vehicle and had opened it with the keys that he had in his possession. A forensic examination had been carried out and a FSL report dated 08.11.2018 established that the chassis number had been tampered through metallic filling. The Additional Sessions Judge in the superdari order took note of the fact that the chassis number revealed after the chemical examination was close to that reflected in the registration documents as only two digits could not be made out. The Tribunal by judgment dated 13.11.2024 set-aside the Order-in- Original. The Tribunal noted that the vehicle owner had discharged the burden in terms of Section 187 of the Customs Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 20 Act by producing the registration book and the auction documents through which the vehicle had been purchased. It noted that the burden of proof then shifted to the Customs Department, which failed to discharge such burden by establishing that the vehicle was brought into Pakistan through an unauthorized route. And that on the basis of FSL report dated 13.02.2024 that the chassis number had been tampered with, a finding could not be rendered that the vehicle was smuggled. The Tribunal found that no one could be deprived of property without establishment of wrongdoing. In view of the facts of the case, it could not be ruled out that the vehicle had been tampered by the Car Lifter. And that the vehicle owner had established that he was the last owner and possessor of the vehicle and had provided the relevant documents to establish that the vehicle had been purchased through an Amnesty Scheme Auction, and there existed no other claimant of such vehicle.

Scope of Reference Jurisdiction 16. Section 196(1) of the Customs Act vests in an aggrieved person and/or Collector/Director of Intelligence & Investigation/Director of Valuation the right to prefer an application against an order of the Tribunal before the High Court “stating any question of law arising out of such order.” Section 196(5) of the Customs Act then provides that the High Court, “shall decide the question of law raised by the reference and pass judgment thereon specifying the grounds on which such judgment is based and the Tribunal's order shall stand modified accordingly.” As has been stated in the introductory part of this judgment, the grounds on which this judgment is Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 21 based include, inter alia, application of provisions of the Constitution, as enumerated by case law, and interpretation of provisions of the Customs Act. It would therefore be beneficial to consider the scope of reference jurisdiction for this Court to satisfy itself that in articulating or answering the questions of law through this judgment the Court has not exceeded its jurisdiction.

17. The language of Section 196 of the Customs Act is similar to the language used in Section 47 of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (“Sales Tax Act”), and Section 133 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“Income Tax Ordinance”). The scope of reference jurisdiction of the High Court under these provisions, as enunciated by the Supreme Court, is therefore relevant while interpreting the scope of reference jurisdiction for purposes of Section 196 of the Customs Act.

18. The Supreme Court up until F.M.Y Industries Ltd. vs. Deputy Commissioner Income Tax (2014 SCMR 907) took a restrictive view of the High Court's reference jurisdiction under various fiscal statutes. This view was reconsidered by the Supreme Court in Messrs Squibb Pakistan Pvt. Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax (2017 SCMR 1006). The Supreme Court while tracing the history of jurisprudence that had evolved on the scope of reference jurisdiction, while considering the provisions of income tax statutes in relation to which case law had evolved, restated the scope of reference jurisdiction in Squibb Pakistan as follows:

48. To recapitulate, the problem all along has been the unfortunate legacy of the Act, 1918. This provided a true illustration of advisory jurisdiction, since advice was to be rendered to the Revenue Authority prior to its having passed Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 22 an order. In 1922, this advisory jurisdiction was retained under section 66(1) of the Act, 1922 which was similarly framed. However, this subsection had, in sum and substance, lost its importance because of subsection (2), which conferred the right to challenge the decision of the Tribunal on questions of law. It was this remedy which was followed thereafter. Section 66(1) ibid thereafter became redundant for all practical purposes and was eventually deleted through a subsequent amendment in 1939 and the same position continued under the Ordinance, 1979 and succeeding law. Thereafter, no advisory jurisdiction remained in any shape or form. But since the significance of the change was not appreciated, the concept of advisory jurisdiction continued to confuse the courts the corpus had disappeared, but the shadow remained. The law as it stands after the 2005 amendment is now clear beyond any conceptual doubt. There is no question of advisory jurisdiction (which phrase was never used in the law at any stage) and the plain words of the section must now be given their ordinary meaning. No hyper technicalities now stand as barriers in the way of substantive justice.

49. An independent interpretation of section 133 of the Ordinance, 2001, as it stands today, on the plain language of the law, liberated from the burden or benefit of earlier judgments, would make the position very clear. Subsection (1) confers a right on any person or the Commissioner aggrieved by a final order of the Appellate Tribunal to file an application before the High Court along with a statement of the case stating any questions of law arising out of the Tribunal's order. There is a direct right to approach the High Court in a similar manner as in appeals, revisions, reviews etc. The order being challenged is the final order but the challenge is limited to questions of law only. The statement must set out the facts, the Tribunal's determination and the questions of law which arise out of its order in terms of subsection (3). The questions of law which may be referred are only those which "arise" out of the order of the Tribunal. On the plain language of the law, this would include any question which can be made out from the order of the Tribunal. There is nothing in the scheme of the section to impute any extraordinary limitations on the type of questions which may be posed. The facts as stated in the Tribunal's order have to be taken as recorded and any question which can be made out from those facts may be raised in an application under section 133 ibid, regardless of whether it was Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 23 previously urged or not. There is absolutely no reason for confining the questions which may be referred to only those which were argued before the Tribunal on the hypothesis that this is an advisory jurisdiction as that is not what the language of the law contemplates. The law, as it stands, allows all questions "arising” out of the order to be referred and not just questions "argued" or "raised” before the Tribunal.

19. The Supreme Court in Pakistan Television Corporation Limited vs. Commissioner Inland Revenue (Legal), LTU, Islamabad (2017 SCMR 1136) went even further and held that, “undoubtedly, a reference under section 133 of the Ordinance would lie before the High Court on a question of law only, however, in the instant cases, the issues (and in the statement of case) before the High Court required an interpretation of various provisions of the Ordinance including sections 21, 153 and 233 which were essentially questions of law. We have examined the order of the Tribunal and find that the above questions of law do arise therefrom, resultantly the tax references before the learned High Court were maintainable.”

20. The misimpression and confusion in some quarters that a tax reference invokes advisory jurisdiction of the High Court and therefore the High Court is bound to answer the question of law brought before it is a misconception and is hereby dispelled.”

21. The Islamabad High Court in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Legal Zone, Large Taxpayers Office vs. M/s Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 24 Wateen Telecom Ltd. etc. (2021 PTD 1827), while summarizing the law laid down by the Supreme Court, held as follows:
(1) Proceedings before the High Court under section 133 of the Ordinance are appellate proceedings.

(2) The decision of the Tribunal in its capacity as the second appellate authority is final to the extent of factual controversies between the parties. The High Court, in proceedings under section 133 of the Ordinance, is to proceed to adjudicate questions of law on the basis of the facts as determined by the Tribunal.

(3) The High Court, in proceedings under section 133 of the Ordinance, may decide any question of law emanating from the proceedings before the Tribunal and is not bound to consider only such questions that arise from the order passed by the Tribunal.

22. The question of the extent to be which the factual determinations made by the Tribunal can be impugned before the High Court has also remained a matter of discussion. In Pakistan Match Industries (Pvt.) 23. Similarly, in Commissioner of Inland Revenue, Lahore vs. Sargodha Spinning Mills (Pvt.) 24. In The Collector of Sales Tax and Central Excise, Lahore vs. Qadbros Engineering (Pvt.) Ltd., Lahore (2023 SCMR 939), the Supreme Court explained that, “the elementary characteristic of this jurisdiction is that it has been conferred to deal only with questions of law and not questions of fact. When we talk of a question of law, it connotes a tangible and substantial question of law on the rights and obligations of the parties founded on the decision of the Tribunal.”

25. The use of the term aggrieved person in Section 196(1) of the Customs Act is not without purpose. The High Court, while considering an application filed by an aggrieved person against an order of the Tribunal, cannot pretend to be engaging in an academic exercise merely because the scope of its jurisdiction is limited to adjudicating questions of law. As explained by the Supreme Court in Qadbros Engineering, the outcome reached by the Tribunal affects the rights and obligations of the relevant parties and the questions of law being adjudicated by the Court similarly affect the rights of such parties by virtue of modifying the order of the Tribunal in terms of Section 196(5) of the Customs Act. The Supreme Court clarified in Pakistan Television Corporation, cited above, that interpretation of provisions of a statute is a question of law and it falls within the domain of the High Court to undertake statutory interpretation where the outcome produced, that affects the rights and obligations of the parties, is contingent on such interpretation. And Squibb Pakistan has clarified that, ―no hyper technicalities now stand as barriers in the way of substantive justice.” Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 26 26. The hierarchy of the sources of law that affects the rights and obligations of parties are well settled when it comes to the application of law by municipal Courts. The Constitution remains the foremost source of law and the provisions of a statute in conflict with the prescriptions of the Constitution must give way to the latter. Similarly, provisions of any Rules and Regulations, sometimes referred to as subordinate legislation, and any administrative instructions issued in exercise of delegated authority flowing from provisions of the statute, must be interpreted such that they are in consonance with the object and language of the parent statute. It is also a well understood proposition that within a common law jurisdiction, the Courts of law are vested with inherent jurisdiction to interpret and apply relevant provisions of law, whether rooted in the Constitution or statutory law, while adjudicating the disputes brought before them. It is in this context that the reference jurisdiction of the High Court in terms of Section 196 of the Customs Act is to be understood. This reference jurisdiction is vested in the Division Bench of a Constitutional Court to uphold the principle of separation of powers in terms of Article 175 of the Constitution, while rendering dispositive decisions. It is a misconception that merely because the adjudication of a question of law requires application of constitutional principles or statutory interpretation or the manner of exercise of statutory authority delegated by the Legislature to the Executive, that such adjudication would fall beyond the scope of reference jurisdiction. As an appellate forum exercising judicial power that impinges on the rights and obligations of parties before it, the High Court cannot remain oblivious to the hierarchy of sources of law that need to be taken account of while answering a question of law brought to it. A Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 27 Division Bench of the High Court exercising reference jurisdiction remains a High Court in terms of Article 192 of the Constitution. It can always exercise another jurisdiction vested by the Constitution or the law to mold and grant relief where the facts and circumstances of the case so dictate. But it need not exercise writ jurisdiction or convert a reference into a writ merely because the question of law that arises from the proceedings and/or order of the Tribunal brought before it in reference jurisdiction requires constitutional and/or statutory interpretation. Such interpretation falls squarely within its scope when so required to answer a question of law properly brought before it in terms of Section 196 of the Custom Act. The scope of Section 187A of the Customs Act 27. The Legislature through the Finance Act, 2025, has introduced Section 187A into the Customs Act, which states the following:

187A. Presumption of legal character of vehicle. - Where any vehicle is detained or seized under this Act or the rules made thereunder and such vehicle upon forensic examination is found to be having a tampered chassis number or cut and weld chassis or chassis number filled with welding material or re-stamped, such vehicle shall be presumed to be smuggled, even if registered with Motor Registration Authority, and shall be confiscated and the Board may authorize the use of such confiscated vehicles for operational purposes in the manner provided in section 182, of this Act, within ninety days of confiscation.

28. During the course of arguments as to what constitutes smuggling in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, Section 187A of the Customs Act was relied on by the learned counsels representing the Customs Department. It was argued that Section 187A of the Customs Act being an explanatory provision Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 28 would apply retrospectively even though it became a part of law as of July 2025. It is therefore essential to consider the scope of Section 187A of the Customs Act and whether a forensic examination report concluding that a vehicle has a tampered chassis number, whether by virtue of the chassis plate being cut and welded or the chassis number being filled with welding material or being re-stamped, is conclusive proof that the vehicle is smuggled, vesting in the State the authority to confiscate such vehicle and use it for operational purposes in terms of Section 182 of the Customs Act.

29. There are a few points to be noted in view of the language used in Section 187A of the Customs Act: One, Section 187A of the Customs Act is in the nature of a deeming clause that creates a presumption that a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is smuggled even if such vehicle is registered with a MRA. Two, it purportedly vests in the Federal Board of Revenue (“FBR”) the power to authorize the use of such confiscated vehicle for operational purposes in terms of Section 182 of the Customs Act. And three, it prescribes a timeline for such authorization, by stating that the same can be granted within 90 days of confiscation. In this part of the judgment, we will only deal with the scope of a deeming provision. We will consider the scope of FBR‘s power to authorize the use of confiscated vehicles later in this judgment while considering the scope of the power created by Sections 169(4) and 182 of the Customs Act together with the scope of CGOs issued in exercise of authority under Section 223 of the Customs Act. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 29 30. In Mehreen Zaibun Nisa vs. Land Commissioner, Multan and others (PLD 1975 SC 397), the Supreme Court summarized the effect of deeming clauses as follows: (i) When a statute contemplates that a state of affairs should be deemed to have existed, it clearly proceeds on the assumption that in fact it did not exist at the relevant time but by a legal fiction we are to assume as if it did exist. (ii) Where a statute says that you must imagine the state of affairs, it does not say that having done so you must cause or permit your imagination to boggle when it comes to the inevitable corollaries of that state of affairs.
(iii) At the same time, it cannot be denied that the Court has to determine the limits within which and the purposes for which the Legislature has created the fiction.

(iv) When a statute enacts that something shall be deemed to have been done which in fact and in truth was not done, the Court is entitled and bound to ascertain for what purposes and between what persons the statutory fiction is to be resorted to."

31. In Begum B. H Syed vs. Mst. Afzal Jehan Begum (PLD 1970 SC 29), the Supreme Court explained that it fell within the Province of the Court, “to determine the limits within which and the purpose for which the Legislature has created a fiction.”

32. While considering the scope of a deeming clause under provisions of the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959, the Supreme Court in Muhammad Yasin vs. Sheikh Ghulam Murtaza and another (PLD 1988 SC 163) held that the power of a Rent Controller to execute an order in the manner of a decree included the power to decide objections while doing so. It noted that the deeming provisions vesting in the Controller the power to execute an order in the manner of a decree of a Civil Court was to be taken to its logical conclusion Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 30 and that the deeming clause, ”has to be given full effect and the logical consequence of the empowering provision must follow.”
33. In Muhammad Mubeen-us-Salam and others v.

Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Defence and others (PLD 2006 SC 602), the Supreme Court considered the scope of a deeming provision at length and cited with approval S.M. Zafar's commentary in Understanding Statutes (2 nd Edition, PP at 101). It went on to observe that, “two important concepts have been introduced by the learned author in the construction of the provision creating a statutory fiction, namely; “statutory fiction should be carried to its logical conclusion as held in Muhammad Yasin v. Sheikh Ghulam Murtaza and another (PLD 1988 SC 163) but the fiction cannot be extended beyond the language of the section by which it is created or by importing another fiction,” therefore, to find a solution, it has been observed that “principle of harmonization shall be attracted” and ultimately it was held that “the impact of deeming clause could be curtailed if it produces a disgraceful result.” The Supreme Court reiterated that it remained for the Court to determine the limits and the purpose for which the Legislature had created a legal fiction by virtue of a deeming clause.

34. In All Pakistan Newspaper Society and others vs. Federation of Pakistan and others (PLD 2012 SC 01), the Supreme Court once again emphasized that the fiction created by a deeming clause could not be extended beyond the language of the Section by which it was created.

35. The aforesaid principles of interpretation in relation to a deeming clause were reiterated in Syed Muddasar Shah Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 31 Termizi vs. Peshawar High Court, Peshawar through Registrar, Peshawar (2021 SCMR 116) and Pak Leather Crafts Limited vs. Al-Baraka Bank Pakistan Limited (2022 SCMR 1868).
36. In Mushtaque Ahmed Memon and another vs.

Arshad Hussain Bhutto and others (2023 SCMR 174), it was held that a deeming clause, “has to be accepted to the extent which it is in conformity with the original Act.” In Dr. Abdul Nabi, Professor, Department of Chemistry, University of Balochistan, Quetta vs. Executive Officer, Cantonment Board, Quetta (2023 SCMR 1267), the Supreme Court held that, “in order to interpret the statute, the Court is obligated to give effect to the deeming provisions while taking into consideration the object of such legal fiction and also dredge up the rationales of statutory fiction to its cogent finale vis-à-vis the intention of legislature so it should not cause any injustice.” The Supreme Court noted that, “the classic statement as to the effect of a deeming clause is to be found in the observations of Lord Asquith in East End Dwelling Company Ltd. vs. Finsbury Borough Council that “where the statute says that you must imagine the state of affairs, it does not say that having done so you must cause or permit your imagination to boggle when it comes to inevitable corollaries of that state of affairs.”

37. In Messrs Shan Traders, Lahore vs. Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Lahore and 2 others (2007 PTD 512), the Division Bench of the Lahore High Court noted that “a deeming clause in a taxation statute must be construed very strictly”.

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 32 38. The first point to note for our purposes is that Section 187A of the Customs Act does not seek to define or redefine smuggling or augment the definition provided in terms of section 2(s) of the Customs Act. It is for purposes of adjudicating the questions of law before the Court and what material/evidence is sufficient to render a determination of smuggling, that this Court is required to interpret the scope of Section 187A of the Customs Act, as a deeming clause, and the purpose for which the Legislature created a legal fiction through such clause. In doing so, this Court must interpret such provision harmoniously with other provisions of the Customs Act, such that the interpretation attributed to Section 187A of the Customs Act neither produces ‗injustice‘ nor ‗a disgraceful result‘. The deeming provision within Section 187A of the Customs Act is part of a fiscal statute. What is more is that in terms of Section 2(s) read with Sections 15, 16, 17, 168, 182 and 156 of the Customs Act, the consequence of a finding that a vehicle is smuggled are penal in nature and result in confiscation of such vehicle together with the possibility of the owner of such vehicle being prosecuted for an offence in terms of Section 156 of the Customs Act. It is therefore essential to construe such deeming provision strictly, such that it promotes the objects of the Customs Act, is interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Customs Act, including Sections 2(s) of the Customs Act that defines the term smuggling, and does not produce any unjust or disgraceful result.

39. According to its preamble, the Customs Act was promulgated to, “consolidate and amend the law relating to the levy and collection of customs duties, fee and service charges Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 33 and to provide for other allied matters.” Such allied matters include preventing and deterring smuggling of goods into Pakistan and prosecuting those found liable for the offence of smuggling or that of possessing/dealing with smuggled goods. In interpreting Section 187A of the Customs Act, it must therefore be borne in mind that while introducing such provision, the Legislature did not seek to bring any amendment to the definition of the word ‗smuggle‘ as provided under section 2(s) of the Customs Act. What constitutes smuggling and when can a good be characterized as being smuggled would continue to be controlled by the definition provided in Section 2(s) of the Customs Act.

40. One interpretation of Section 187A of the Customs Act could be that any vehicle, whether imported or locally manufactured in Pakistan, if found to have a tampered chassis number would qualify as a smuggled vehicle. This interpretation would raise questions about the constitutionality of such provision as it could be seen as removing a causal link between a wrongful act (i.e. smuggling a vehicle into Pakistan), and the penal consequence of such act (i.e. confiscation of the vehicle and prosecution of the smuggler or person in possession of such smuggled vehicle). Such interpretation would not promote the object of the Customs Act, which is to control, prevent and deter smuggling as defined in Section 2(s) of the Customs Act. A vehicle that is locally manufactured and/or has been legally imported into Pakistan after payment of duties and taxes cannot be characterized as a smuggled vehicle merely because its chassis number has been defaced or tampered for reasons other than that of hiding the true identity of a smuggled vehicle. To Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 34 slap penal consequences such as confiscation of property or criminal prosecution on the owner of a vehicle on the sole basis that vehicle‘s chassis number is tampered, when there is logical explanation for such tampering and/or the owner is not liable for the act of tampering, would most certainly produce an unjust and disgraceful result, which the Legislature could most certainly not have intended. It is also understood that locally manufactured vehicles, that are not imported, fall beyond the scope of provisions of the Customs Act. Section 187A of the Customs Act can therefore not be given a meaning that would result in an absurdity i.e. result in the declaration of a locallymanufactured vehicle as a smuggled vehicle merely because its chassis number has been tampered.

41. It is in this context that the deeming provision of Section 187A of the Customs Act must be given a restrictive meaning, for being a provision within a fiscal statute creating penal consequences. It must be understood as vesting in the FBR and the Customs Department jurisdiction in relation to a vehicle with a tampered chassis number by virtue of creating a presumption that such vehicle may be smuggled. But for such provision, Customs Authorities may arguably not be vested with jurisdiction to exercise their police powers to detain and seize vehicles and initiate adjudicatory proceedings for purposes of confiscation in relation to vehicles that are registered with the MRA and have not been freshly imported. Section 187A of the Customs Act is therefore to be understood as a deeming provision vesting jurisdiction in the Customs Authorities to exercise powers in relation to vehicles with tampered chassis numbers, which power, but for such deeming provision, would ordinarily vest in Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 35 police authorities and MRA. Notwithstanding such jurisdictionvesting provision, Section 2(s) of the Customs Act would continue to control what constitutes a smuggled good and the ultimate legal onus to prove that a vehicle is smuggled would remain with the State, subject to the requirements of Section 187 read with Section 156 of the Customs Act, as will be explained later in this judgment. The presumption created by Section 187A of the Customs Act would thus be a rebuttable presumption and the mere fact that a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is purportedly registered with a MRA would not be dispositive of the fact that such vehicle is not smuggled. Civil forfeiture and constitutional right to property 42. Within our jurisprudence there has been no extensive analysis of whether or not penalties imposed in terms of Section 156 of the Customs Act in the form of civil forfeiture of property, impinges on the constitutional right to property guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution. And to the extent that the consequence of civil forfeiture (without a criminal trial of the person deemed liable for the offence of smuggling or for the offence of possessing a smuggled item) constitutes a penalty, in what circumstances can an individual not liable for an offence be deprived of his property while upholding the guarantees of due process and fair trial in terms of Article 10A of the Constitution?

43. We need to undertake a three-tier analysis for our present purpose. As step one, we will consider imposition of penalty in terms of Section 156 of the Customs Act that is in the nature of civil forfeiture of property and the constitutional and/or policy concerns such penal action raise. Step two would be to consider the nature of property rights guaranteed by the Constitution and Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 36 whether Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution afford any protection to an individual suspected of possessing property that is deemed to be smuggled. And step three would be to consider the requirements for attribution of liability and imposition of penalty on an individual who is not deemed to be guilty as a person, but is the owner of property that is deemed to be guilty and liable to confiscation. Civil forfeiture is understood to be an action against property. It is therefore referred to as a consequence of proceedings in rem as opposed to proceedings against the person referred to as proceedings in personam. By virtue of civil forfeiture the State ordinarily seeks to confiscate proceeds of criminal activity in order to deprive the possessor of the property of illicit gains without initiating criminal proceedings against an individual.

44. Civil forfeiture, as a consequence of proceedings in rem, has its roots in common law. Through such action the Crown would traditionally bring proceedings in the Court of Exchequer to obtain a judicial decree to seek recognition of its ownership of items of property. The Court of Exchequer was the forum in England for actions to enforce forfeitures under customs statutes (see for example Daniel Howard, A Treatise on Summary Proceedings under the Law of Excise and Customs, London, 1812). Civil forfeitures came to be seen as a legal means authorizing proceedings in rem against ‗property‘ that was ‗guilty‘ in the eyes of law. While historically the use of in rem process was restricted to property itself involved in illegal conduct, over time such process has also been employed in various jurisdictions against property acquired as a result of illegal conduct.

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 37 45. The policy argument in support of civil forfeiture has been that it remains an effective means to recover assets derived from criminal or unlawful activity without the need to seek criminal conviction of an individual found guilty of criminal or illegal conduct. Thus, where guilt can be assigned to property for being a product of criminal or illegal activity, the State seeks to claim ownership of such property as a means to prevent illicit or unjust enrichment by organized crime and to suppress conditions that incentivize unlawful activities. The critique of such approach to legal enforcement is that it infringes on property rights, enables the State to impose penalties on property owners without affording them the protections that due process within the criminal justice system mandates, and creates a lazy alternative for the State to take confiscatory action without the need to establish wrongdoing beyond reasonable doubt. These legal and policy concerns have resulted in legal actions challenging the scope and legitimacy of civil forfeitures and various jurisdictions have come up with their own tests to ensure that civil forfeiture is undertaken such that it does not breach fundamental rights to property and due process, and that the punishment is proportionate to the wrongdoing that the State seeks to prevent.

46. The European Court of Human Rights employs a three-pronged test to ensure that there is no breach of constitutionally protected property rights when it comes to civil forfeiture. The three questions it asks are: is the measure lawful (i.e. provided for by Domestic Law); is it directed towards a legitimate aim (i.e. is it justified by State necessity); and is the measure proportionate to the ill that it seeks to prevent. It is Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 38 through this three-part test that a balance is struck between the interests of the person suffering the forfeiture and the interests of the community in preventing and deterring criminal/illegal conduct.

47. The Courts in United Kingdom (UK) apply the proportionality test to ensure that civil forfeiture does not arbitrarily interfere with property rights. An exception to the penalty of forfeiture is available where the property may be traceable to a crime, but the owner in question acquired it in good faith, for full value, without notice of the crime. Other common law jurisdictions employ similar protections to create exceptions to civil forfeiture. Canada allows ―interests of justice‖ and ―legitimate owner‖ defences. New Zealand and Australia similarly allow ―undue hardship‖ defences. In the United States (U.S.), the burden to initiate a forfeiture case was historically not too high. However, since promulgation of the Civil Assets Forfeiture Reform Act, 2000, it is now for the State to prove its case on a balance of probabilities. And the law also provides for an ―innocent owner defence‖ (i.e. where an owner can establish that he/she had no knowledge that the property had been used in a crime or was a product of proceeds of crime, and had acquired the property in good faith at full value without notice of its criminal origin, such property is not liable for confiscation).

48. The academic commentaries in relation to States initiating in rem proceedings to affect civil forfeiture flag the constitutional concern that rendering dispositive judgments that have the effect of confiscating property fall within the province of the judiciary and such forfeitures must only be given effect when the decision to confiscate has been scrutinized and upheld by the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 39 judicial branch of the State. It is also pointed out that where law permits enforcement agencies to retain the property confiscated through civil forfeiture or put it to its own use, such incentives create a conflict of interest that adversely affect enforcement priorities and enforcement methods. The incentivization of civil forfeiture creates an alternative to criminal prosecution, as the lower standard of proof for confiscating property (without bringing home a charge against an individual beyond reasonable doubt) is an easy way out for law enforcement agencies. And where its effect is to deprive an innocent owner of his/her property and benefits individuals within the law enforcement agency, who retain or derive direct or indirect benefits from such forfeiture, the norms of honest policing and the underlying object of deterring criminal activity and preventing unjust enrichment are undermined.

49. There is scant case law on the scope and constitutionality of in rem civil forfeiture in Pakistan. While the question of constitutionality of civil forfeitures has not been raised before us in these matters, we will briefly consider cases where civil forfeiture has been considered or alluded to in our jurisprudence. And in such context, we will consider the right to private property as philosophically understood and as guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution and whether civil forfeiture impinges on such right where the owner of goods/vehicles is not found liable for wrongdoing.

50. The most coherent account of how departmental proceedings leading to confiscation of goods qualify as proceedings in rem is provided in Punjab Cables vs. Government of Pakistan (PLD 1989 Lahore 121), where the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 40 Lahore High Court borrowed the jurisprudence from India while enumerating clause (9) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act as follows:

“It is obvious from this provision that two penalties are provided; one relating to the goods, which are liable to confiscation, and the other relating to the person concerned, who is liable to a penalty not exceeding twice the value of the goods. Section 167(8) of the Sea Customs Act, 1978, which is a somewhat similar provision, was discussed by the Supreme Court of India in Sewpunjanrai Indrasanarai Ltd. v. Collector of Customs (AIR 1958 S.C. 845), where it was held that proceedings so far as they related to the confiscation of the goods were basically proceedings in rem, as the penalty was enforced against the goods, whether the offender was known or not known, and that the order of confiscation under section 182 of the Sea Customs Act operated directly upon the status of the property and by virtue of section 184 it transferred an absolute title to Government. It is, therefore, clear that proceedings under section 156(1)(9) of the Customs Act, 1969, are proceedings in rem, that the penalty is enforced against the goods and that the order of confiscation operates directly upon the status of the property, in view of section 182 of the Act, which clearly states that when goods are confiscated, they shall forthwith vest in the Federal Government and the officer who orders confiscation shall take and hold possession of the same.”

51. The other judgment that has been cited to explain how departmental proceedings leading to confiscation are distinguishable from criminal proceedings before the Special Judge is Adam vs. Collector of Customs, Karachi (PLD 1969 SC 446), wherein it was held as follows:

“The intention of the Legislature is thus clear that the disposal of the goods seized under the Sea Customs Act is left entirely in the jurisdiction of the customs authorities. The proceedings taken by the customs authorities for the confiscation of the goods are more in the nature of departmental proceedings which have been characterized in English and American jurisprudence as proceedings in condemnation of the goods for Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 41 purposes of revenue and are regarded as proceedings of a civil nature, despite their penal character.”

The Supreme Court went on to hold that as the two remedies were independent of each other, “no question of double jeopardy arises when simultaneously or subsequently a trial is held to determine the guilt of the individual, who has been concerned in the offences in respect of the goods, which are the subjectmatter of the adjudication proceedings.” Adam has been cited at length by the Sindh High Court in Shoukat Ali v. Special Judge (Customs and Taxation) (PTCL 2014 Cl. 141) to reaffirm the power vested in customs authorities to impose fines and order confiscation of property, while also referring to other judgments rendered by the High Courts, following the principle laid down in Adam.

52. The conclusions that can be drawn from the academic and judicial literature available is that a judgment in rem is a judgment against the whole world, which determines rights in the property itself and does not determine the liability of the individual who owns/possesses such property. It is thus that a finding that a property is liable to be confiscated for being the product of a criminal or illegal activity, when rendered in rem, does not amount to imposition of penalty on the individual who claims to be the owner of such property. And it is in this perspective that proceedings in rem ordering the confiscation of property are treated as proceedings separate from proceedings in personam against an individual deemed liable for an offence of smuggling under provisions of the Customs Act, which proceedings are of a judicial nature and brought before the Special Judge appointed under the Customs Act. The principle cited in support of in rem proceedings is that such proceedings Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 42 merely determine title in property, and as property that is the product of criminal or illegal activity is to be treated as ―guilty property‖, no one can claim clean title in such property. But the missing link in such analysis is why shouldn‘t proceedings in rem ordering confiscation of property also be viewed as imposition of civil penalty on an individual, who claims to be the owner of the property, and consequently in derogation of his/her civil/property rights guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, to the extent that such individual is not found culpable.

53. The relevant question that arises is where no wrongdoing is attributable to or established against the owner of property, can the property itself be confiscated on the basis that the penalty is being imposed on the property and not on the owner? It is in this context that the principle of culpability in relation to any penal sanction becomes relevant, which when read with the three-part test applied by the European Court of Human Rights and the exceptions or defences to confiscation upheld in other jurisdictions, including the defence of ―bonafide purchaser‖ or ―legitimate owner‖ or ―undue hardship‖ begin to make sense as the correct approach to balance the rights of the community in preventing crime and smuggling vis-à-vis the rights of an individual to retain and enjoy his/her property. There appears to be no reasonable or valid legal argument in favor of the proposition that confiscation of property does not constitute a penalty for the property owner deprived of property, or that a property owner can be saddled with penalty without being found culpable in any manner.

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 43 54. “One of the accepted principles for the imposition of a penalty is that there must be some culpability or negligence in the person sought to be made liable. Therefore, if the property of a wholly innocent person had been used without his consent, connivance or even knowledge, it would be grossly unjust to confiscate his property. It could not possibly have been the intention of a Legislature to penalise wholly innocent persons far less could persons be deprived of their property used by others after obtaining possession of the same by unlawful means or under circumstances over which they could not possibly have any control.

Could it be said that if contraband goods were found being carried in a railway carriage, the railway carriage would be liable to confiscation; or, if contraband goods were carried in a Government truck, the Government truck would be liable for confiscation?...

After emphasizing the above principles of natural justice, culpability and proportionality, the Supreme Court found that it had not been established by the customs authorities that the owner of the vehicle had knowledge of illegal or improper use of the vehicle and the confiscation of such vehicle was set-aside.

55. Article 23 of the Constitution vests in every citizen the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property subject to “reasonable restrictions imposed by law in public interest”. Article 24 of the Constitution includes a prohibition against deprivation of property and provides that property cannot be compulsorily acquired except for a public purpose and without making a provision for compensation of such property. For purposes of fiscal laws, the articles guaranteeing property rights have been interpreted to mean that any measure resulting in confiscation of property (except when taken in accordance with law) would be ultra vires the Constitution. And consequently, actions taken under fiscal laws such as taxation when found to be confiscatory are declared ultra vires the Constitution. Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution are read together with Article 9 of the Constitution that guarantees the right of citizens to liberty. In terms of its philosophical origins, the right to private property has been regarded as a subset of the right to liberty, and in the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 45 context of the relationship between the citizen and the State, the protection of property is regarded as an essential feature of the rule of law.

56. John Locke argued in Two Treatises (II, SEC-138) that, “the preservation of property being the end of government, and that for which men enter into society, it necessarily supposes and requires that the people should have property…” From the perspective of liberal thought property rights, alongwith rights to life and liberty, are treated as the basis of political morality in a rule of law system. (See for example G.W.F. Hegel‘s The Philosophy of Right (Oxford University Press, 1967). The acceptance of right to private property is thus logically tied to the rule that expropriation of such property without compensation is prohibited. Jeremy Waldron in The Right to Private Property (2002, Clarendon Press, Oxford, pp. 31) argues that, “the concept of property is the concept of a system of rules governing access to and control of material resources… In all times and places with which we are familiar, material resources are scarce relative to human demands that are made on them.” He argues that while such scarcity prevails, individuals disagree about how to make use of the resources, which raises the problem of allocation: “This is the problem of determining peacefully and reasonably predictably who is to have access to which resources for what purpose and when. The system of social rules, which I call property rules are always solving that problem.” Waldron further argues that, “in a system of private property, the rules governing access to and control of material resources are organized around the idea that resources are on the whole separate objects each assigned and therefore Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 46 belonging to some particular individual”, while highlighting that ―belonging‖ is the ―organizing idea‖ in relation to private property. He continues that, “in a private property system, a rule is laid down that, in case of each object, the individual person whose name is attached to the object is to determine how the object shall be used and by whom. His decision is to be upheld by the society as final.”

57. Our Constitution endorses a system of private property in terms of Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, which rights are not absolute and can be regulated by law in public interest and can even be compulsorily acquired for a public purpose subject to provision of compensation. In the instant matter, the question before us is the circumstances in which control of property in a vehicle can be assigned to the State at the expense of the individual who lays claim to the ownership of such property. And whether such confiscatory action can be explained away as having no relevance to Article 23 and 24 rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The short answer to the question is that a person who is the owner of a property cannot be deprived of such property in disregard of the guarantees in Articles 9, 23 and 24, read together with the guarantees in Article 10A of the Constitution, by creating a fiction that the penalty is imposed on the property itself and not on the individual. It is not in contention that where a vehicle is confiscated for the benefit of the State through in rem proceedings, the effect is the substitution of title in relation to such property (i.e. the property claimed by an individual as his/her own is deemed not to belong to such person by virtue of it being a product of a crime or illegal activity, and the property is declared to vest in the State). Such Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 47 confiscatory action can therefore not be taken while pretending that it does not interfere with the right of a citizen to liberty or property or due process guaranteed by the Constitution. In order for such forfeiture to be seen as a legal and moral act by the State, it must be found that the action leading to confiscation of private property is a reasonable restriction imposed by law in the public interest, and such penalty has been imposed while upholding due process rights of the individual who claims to be the owner of such property, and consequently such action does not fall foul of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution.

58. One of the foundational concepts in the justification of penal systems is the principle of individual autonomy (i.e. each individual is responsible and accountable for his/her own behavior). In Punishment and Responsibility (1968, Oxford University Press) HLA Hart argued that, “an individual ought not be held liable unless he/she had the “capacity” and “opportunity” to do otherwise. Prohibition of conduct in a penal system is rooted in the “harm principle”; the reduction or prevention of harm to others is a legitimate reason to support sanctions.
