In Principles of Criminal Law (1999, Oxford University Press) Professor Andrew Ashworth argues that, “at the heart of the principle of autonomy lies the idea of respect for individuals as rational, choosing persons... that an individual should only be held criminally liable for consequences that were knowingly brought about or knowingly risked. The principle of culpability is Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 48 therefore equally attracted even in relation to an offence of possession.”

60. A person must not be punished if no wrongdoing can be attributed to him/her. Calling the punishment one against property (in rem) as opposed to one against the person (in personam) doesn't help get around the right to possession and enjoyment of property as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution. Equally important is the voluntariness requirement of wrongdoing, which comes alongwith the requirement of establishing causation. In other words, without focus on causation and the culpability of an individual being subjected to a penal sanction, the penal system would stop being a mechanism for social control designed to inform and regulate the conduct of individuals within the society as rational beings, and would degenerate into an arbitrary punishment system. The legal system established in accordance with the provisions of our Constitution is also based on individual responsibility for action. Any penal scheme established under it requires, as a first step, the attribution of wrongdoing to an individual before he/she can be burdened with a penalty.

61. It is at the stage of determination of wrongdoing that questions about guilty act (actus reus) and guilty intent (mens rea) are asked. Once the question of culpability or wrongdoing is settled, the system moves on to stage two, which deals with the question of sanctions to be imposed on the wrongdoing. To argue that an individual can be deprived of his property by imposition of a penal sanction under provisions of the Customs Act without any attribution of culpability or wrongdoing to the property owner would amount to stating that our Constitution Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 49 permits imposition of penalty without attribution or finding of culpability. This cannot be countenanced. To the extent that confiscation acts as a punishment, whether as a consequence of departmental/adjudicatory proceedings resulting in civil forfeiture or as a consequence of punishment after conviction, the penalty must be a consequence flowing from a finding of wrongdoing to pass constitutional muster.

62. The next question that arises is that of proportionality i.e. is the penalty imposed proportionate to the mischief that is sought to be curbed in public interest? We note here that the constitutional jurisprudence that has evolved in Pakistan supports an endorsement of the three-part test that has been articulated by the European Court of Human Rights while considering the legality of civil forfeiture. The first prong of such test (detailed earlier in this judgment) requires that the principle of legality be satisfied. Article 4 of the Constitution provides that the State can only do what it is authorized by law to do. Likewise, Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution also provide that a citizen cannot be deprived of property except when property is taken in accordance with law. Under our constitutional scheme, the state can only impinge on property rights of an individual when authorized by law to do so.

63. The second prong of the three-part test is that deprivation of property (i.e. confiscation) satisfies the requirement of necessity. In our context this means that confiscation promotes the objects of the Customs Act and is necessary for achieving the purpose for which such penal sanction has been created by the Legislature. The third prong in the three-part test is to Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 50 ensure that the sanction imposed is proportionate to the mischief that is sought to be prevented or deterred.

64. There are a few principles of statutory interpretation, when it comes to application of statutory law within a realm inhabited by constitutionally protected rights, that are well settled. 84. This fact sequence in a case of civil forfeiture also raises questions related to causation and proportionality. What public interest would confiscation of private property serve when it has the effect of taking property away from a citizen and vesting it in the State, in circumstances where the citizen is neither to blame for the illegality in question nor would such action have the effect of preventing and/or deterring future illegal activity such as smuggling?

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 59 85. One of the objects of the penal system is to seek retribution from somebody found culpable of wrongdoing. Another object of the penal system is to deter malefactors from wrongdoing in the future. However, if penalty is imposed on an innocent person as opposed to a malefactor, such action neither promotes public interest in seeking retribution nor in deterring illegal conduct in the future, as there is no causal link between the illegal act being punished and the person left to bear the consequences of such act. It is in view of these competing interests that the question of (i) whether or not the property sought to be confiscated by the State is the product of illegal activity, (ii) whether the person who is the owner of such property is a bonafide purchaser for full value without notice of any deficiency of title, become relevant matters of evidence.

88. The question of where the onus of proof lies in a case where proceedings for confiscation of smuggled property have been initiated has remained a matter of much debate. Let us start with the basics. The standard principle in criminal law is that every person is deemed innocent until proven guilty in accordance with law. Article 122 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (“QSO”), provides that, “when any fact is especially within the knowledge of any person, the burden of proving that fact is upon him.” Let us also reproduce here Article 126 of the QSO, which states that, “when the question is whether any person is owner of anything of which he is shown to be in possession, the burden of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who affirms that he is not the owner.”

The manner in which the burden of proof continues to shift under provisions of the Customs Act was considered by the Sindh High Court in Kamran Industries vs. Collector of Customs (PTCL 1996 CL 15), wherein it was held that, “on a closer scrutiny of the provisions of Section 187 and the case law settled by our courts on the subject it appears that in such a Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 64 situation it is only the evidential and tactical burden of proof which is cast upon the accused while the legal burden to bring home the allegations remains with the prosecution.”

95. The Sindh High Court explained in Abdul Razzaq vs. Directorate General of Intelligence and Investigation-FBR, Regional Office, Karachi and 2 others (2016 PTD 1861) that, “the evidential and tactical burden being initially placed on the accused in a Customs offence is now well settled law as is the principle that the accused only needs to show some evidence to prima facie discharge his evidential burden and thereafter the same will shift on the Customs authorities.”

96. The manner in which legal and evidential burden is to be distinguished and understood, and how the best evidence rule works, was summarized by the Islamabad High Court, after scrutinizing relevant case law, in Messrs Naseem & Company and others vs. Capital Development Authority and others (2022 MLD 1426), wherein the Court's findings were summarized as follows:

i) Burden of proof has two interrelated but distinct facets: legal burden and evidential burden. The former remains on a party throughout the trial. It is the outcome of the entirety of the evidence before a court, regardless from which party or source the evidence originates. The evidential burden however is a shifting phenomenon. It is meant to originate from the party alleging the existence of certain facts, but may shift to the other party as the trial progresses.

ii) The best evidence rule postulates that each party must produce all material evidence in its possession or power and failure to do so entitles the court to draw an adverse inference against the party failing to produce it. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 65 97. In Abdul Qadir vs. The Additional Collector Customs (Customs Reference No.44 of 2015) this Court relied on the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Nazakat Khan vs. The Collector of Customs, Custom House, Peshawar (Civil Appeal No.452 of 2015, judgment dated 16.02.2021) to reiterate that tampering of a Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) was not synonymous with smuggling. Further relying on the law laid down by the Sindh High Court in Kamran Industries and Abdul Razzaq vs. Director General Intelligence and Investigation-FBR, Regional Office Karachi and 2 others (2016 PTD 1861), this Court noted that, “no doubt that the initial burden of proof to show that any act done by or anything in possession of an accused is with lawful authority or under a permit, license or other document prescribed by any law is upon the accused person under Section 187 of the Act. However, it is now well settled that it is only the evidential and tactical burden which is initially placed on the accused in a customs offence and that the accused need only show some evidence to prima facie discharge his evidential burden and thereafter the onus shifts upon the customs authorities.” The Court further clarified that where the owner of the vehicle, “is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubt, the benefit of such doubt must go to the accused whereas the ultimate burden remains on the customs authorities to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt as was explained in the case of Collector Customs, Sales Tax and Central Excise, Customs House, Quetta Vs. Naimtullah, 2003 PTD 2118, by the Honorable Quetta High Court.” In the facts of the case, the Court concluded that the vehicle owner had discharged his burden of proof in terms of Sections 156(2) and Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 66 187 of the Customs Act while establishing a prima facie case in his favor, whereas the Customs Department had failed to discharge its onus to establish that the vehicle was not duty paid/smuggled. The vehicle was therefore ordered to be released.

98. The Islamabad High Court in Iftikhar Ahmed Khan vs. The Customs Appellate Tribunal and others (Custom Reference No.112 of 2023) ordered the release of a vehicle by judgment dated 22.04.2024. In the said case, a vehicle had been confiscated on the basis that data with regard to import of the vehicle was not available in the PRAL database and the registration documents of the vehicle could not be verified by the Motor Registration Authority in Jacobabad, as the said documentation was destroyed by a fire in the year 2007 amidst riots in the aftermath of the assassination of Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto. The Court held that in the absence of Customs authorities establishing the charge of smuggling in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, the detention of the vehicle was ordered arbitrarily and was therefore not sustainable. The Court also took into account the fact that the Order-in-Original had been issued beyond the period of limitation prescribed in Section 179 of the Customs Act.

99. The latest view of the Supreme Court in relation to, inter alia, manner of proof in a customs case involving confiscation of a vehicle is reflected in The Intelligence Officer, Directorate of Intelligence & Investigation, FBR and others vs. Abdul Karim (2025 SCMR 969). While explaining what constitutes smuggling, the Supreme Court noted that, “for clause 89 [Section 156(1)] to apply, the condition precedent is that the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 67 goods in question should be smuggled. In terms of Section 2(s) read with the applicable notification thereunder it seems that the vehicles can be considered smuggled if either (i) at the relevant time, the applicable notification in terms of Section 2(s)(ii) included vehicles, or (ii) in terms of Section 2(s)(iii) the vehicles were brought in by any route other than a route declared under Section 9 or Section 10 or from any place other than the customs station.” Notwithstanding contrary observations in past judgments, the Supreme Court acknowledged that the doctrine of a bonafide purchaser may apply in a case of smuggling. In relation to how the presumption of a bonafide owner applies in case of a registered vehicle, the Supreme Court held that: “…it is reasonable to assume that if a vehicle stands registered, the government is presumed to have exercised due care and diligence with respect to its obligation to see whatever duties and taxes as payable to the government before a vehicle can be registered, stand paid. It must also be noted that the vehicles being registered, which registration was duly verified, is presumed to have been brought lawfully; after completion of notified period in case of used vehicles also. It seems harsh, to say the least, if without any proof that a person (last owner) was involved in the registration of the vehicle knowing fully well that no duties and taxes, as required under the law, were paid, and therefore the vehicle was fraudulently registered, the vehicle be seized from him on his failure to produce documents of import and payment of duties and taxes thereon and even that beyond the period of three years or five years, as the case may be, as required under section 211(2). In most of the cases since first registration, the vehicles changed many owners on the strength of registration book and no adverse inference could be drawn for the ultimate bonafide owners unless otherwise proved contrary by appellant, in which exercise the appellant department has failed below. The verified registration book and official record is enough for bonafide presumption that a valid title exists... Section 27 of [the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965] even provides the production of the vehicle at the time of registration and if the registration of a vehicle Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 68 passes through this statutory process conducted by officials responsible under M.V.O 1965, then presumption of truthfulness is eminent.”

100. The Supreme Court went on to reiterate the law laid down by the Privy Council back in 1955 to draw a distinction between the term lawful excuse as used in clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act and lawful authority as used in Section 187 of the Customs Act. While emphasizing that, ―lawful excuse is an expression that is of wider import and lesser degree of burden than lawful authority‖, the Supreme Court explained that, “Section 187 in general deals with burden of proof as to lawful authority whereas Section 156 deals with punishment for offence. In this context, Section 187 can be regarded as a general provision whereas clauses (89) and (90) are specific provisions and in such a situation the specific provisions (to the context) must apply to the event/situation under discussion. As such, the accused persons are entitled only to demonstrate a lawful excuse to discharge themselves from the allegation under the said clauses even where the law is conceived to have been violated in respect of the goods i.e. the goods are smuggled goods in absence of import documents, and that is possible courtesy statutory period, (disclosed in Section 211) followed by registration book through an official act under the law. A strong presumption is thus attached as a statutory act was performed in the registration of accused.” The Supreme Court held that expiry of the limitation period prescribed in Section 211 of the Customs Act would provide, a “lawful excuse” to the person (retaining the possession of the vehicle under valid registration), who is accused of an offence under Section 156(89) or (90) (for not showing required import documents), Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 69 unless it can be demonstrated that he was told or knew that duties and taxes were not paid and the same were required to be paid.” And thus, “no adverse inference for failure to produce the documents can be drawn after the lapse of period provided in Section 211(2) to be counted at-least from the date of registration if not before, as auction date in other vehicles is also a legitimate claim to count time.”

101. The Customs Department in the instant cases has relied upon Para-22 of the ruling in Abdul Karim to argue that the law laid down with regard to lawful excuse to possess a vehicle does not apply to vehicles with tampered chassis and engine numbers. Para-22 of the Abdul Karim states the following: “This principle however is distinguished for the case where vehicles were found with tampered chassis and engine numbers. If this is seemingly done to match the statistics of original vehicles auctioned or brought into Pakistan officially having different chassis/engine number, the lawful excuse may not be applicable in case of tampered vehicle. This would not include those vehicles which were acquired via auction report explicitly disclosing such tampering and tampered statistics. Also at times the engine and chassis numbers are changed which are also excluded from any action, provided it was done with prior permission of the authority under the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965. All this require thorough probe at the end to applicant which again is a question of fact not required to be determined by us afresh.”
102. The Supreme Court went on to explain the manner in which the exception was to apply in cases of vehicles with tampered chassis numbers in Para-25 as follows:

“The conclusion in the above analysis is that the vehicles in question are those which were either auctioned or were brought into Pakistan and were registered through a statutory process and that the auction papers or registration papers of some other vehicles are not being used fraudulently, however, Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 70 where it is established that the chassis/engine numbers have been tampered with after auction or registration to match the description of the auctioned or registered vehicle, the lawful excuse is not available.”

103. There are a few key points to note with regard to the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Abdul Karim. The first point is that in view of the limitation period prescribed in Section 211 of the Customs Act, in case of a registered vehicle, no adverse inference in relation to the import or payment of taxes and duties can be drawn after a period of five years from the registration of a vehicle and/or its import/auction. In such cases, a presumption would apply after the registration of the vehicle that the State has discharged its duty to perform due diligence and satisfy itself prior to its registration that the vehicle in question is not smuggled. The second point is that a bonafide purchaser and owner of a vehicle need only establish lawful excuse to be in possession of the vehicle, and production of a valid registration book would discharge such onus. And the third point is that the owner of a tampered vehicle would not be found to have discharged his onus to establish lawful excuse to possess such vehicle, ―where it is established that the chassis/engine numbers have been tampered with after auction or registration to match the description of the auctioned or registered vehicle…‖ The requirement to establish that the tampering of the chassis number has happened after an auction or registration of the vehicle then becomes an evidentiary matter to be established by the Customs Department.

104. What emerges from the above discussion is that where Customs authorities initiate proceedings for confiscation of property in terms of Section 156 of the Customs Act, the initial Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 71 evidential burden to prove on a balance of probabilities that such person has a lawful excuse to possess such property is on the private individual/owner of the vehicle. Once purported owner of the vehicle discharges his/her burden by making out a prima facie case re legal excuse to own/possess the vehicle by producing valid registration with the MRA, the burden shifts back to the State to establish as a legal matter that the State has succeeded in proving on a balance of probabilities that the property in question is smuggled and consequently the product of illegal activity. It is only after the State discharges such onus to prove that the property is tainted with illegality or is a product of crime, and the purported owner fails to discharge the onus of establishing a lawful excuse to own/possess the vehicle, including a defence such as being a bonafide purchaser for full value without notice of any infirmity in the vehicle‘s title backed by a valid registration, that a penalty can be imposed resulting in the confiscation of such vehicle in favor of the State. It is in this context that the interpretation of the term lawful excuse as used in clause (89) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act becomes relevant.

105. The Sindh High Court in The Additional Director, Directorate General of Intelligence and Investigation vs. Imran and another (2021 PTD 1683) considered when private individuals would be deemed to have succeeded in establishing lawful excuse for possession of vehicles that were claimed to be smuggled by the Customs Department. The Sindh High Court observed that where the owner of a vehicle was able to produce the original registration book issued by Motor Vehicle Registration Authority alongwith customs auction documents, Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 72 bank challans and documents reflecting payment of duties and taxes, the vehicle owner would be seen as having discharged the initial burden of proof in terms of Section 187 of the Customs Act. The Sindh High Court further held that in the context of Section 211 of the Customs Act and the duty imposed by it demanding record beyond the period of five years that, “if such authority is given to the public functionaries to charge the owners of the vehicles of a criminal offence of smuggling in the absence of any evidence or material to this effect, would amount to giving unbridled powers to act arbitrarily and to abuse the process of law, which is neither the intent of law nor could be approved by Courts under any circumstances.” The Sindh High Court held that, “in the absence of any material, inquiry/investigation or any steps required to be undertaken for establishing the charge of smuggling in terms of Section 2(s), or to make out a case that owners of the vehicles are found in possession of smuggled vehicles in terms of Sections 156(1), (89) and (90) of the Customs Act, 1969, and even without following the legal course of adjudication as provided under Chapter XIX of the Customs Act, 1969, subject vehicles have been detained/seized on the charges of smuggling. In all these cases, subject vehicles have been detained/confiscated by the Customs Authorities in a highly arbitrary manner while the same were plying within the territorial city limits, in spite of the fact that initial burden to prove the lawful ownership and possession of subject Registered Vehicles was discharged by the owners through production of aforesaid documents.” After documenting such a rebuke, the vehicles were ordered to be released. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 73 106. It was held by the Supreme Court in Nazakat Khan vs. The Collector of Customs, Custom House, Peshawar (Civil Appeal No.452 of 2015), by judgment dated 16.02.2021, in an appeal filed against the judgment of the Peshawar High Court reported as Sultan Muhammad vs. Collector of Customs and another (2015 PTD 570) [which judgment had previously been relied on by the Supreme Court in Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa vs. Sarfraz Khan (2020 SCMR 1410)], that:

“The question is always whether there has been smuggling within the meaning, and for purposes, of the Customs Act. To simply jump from a (factual) conclusion that there has been “tampering” (if such be the case) to the (legal) determination that there must therefore have been smuggling is facile. It must be recognized that the term “tampering” is used in the context of smuggling in a special, and restricted, sense. To put the matter a bit differently, in a context such as the present while every “tampering” may involve an “alteration”, every “alteration” is not “tampering”. These, and related, questions (including as to the correct meaning of S. 156(1), clause (89) of the Customs Act) were not properly raised before the learned High Court and cannot be raised now before us. However, we would leave them open for future consideration in an appropriate case.”

Motor Vehicles Ordinance and Warranties by the State 107. Before we proceed further, let us consider the import of provisions of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965 (“Motor Vehicles Ordinance”) and the effect of registration of a vehicle to comprehend (i) the distinction between tampering and smuggling drawn by the Supreme Court in Nazakat Khan, and (ii) law laid down in Abdul Karim.

108. In view of Nazakat Khan, it is evident that the Customs Department cannot conflate the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 74 Ordinance with those of the Customs Act for the purpose of establishing an offence under the later. The Motor Vehicles Ordinance is a provincial statute administered by the Provincial Governments and provides for independent offences, penalties, and adjudicatory mechanisms. Notwithstanding this clarification, for the purpose of discharge of the onus of proof by a vehicle owner, in a smuggling case built by the Customs authorities, the registration of the vehicle issued by the MRA under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance remains relevant. In terms of Article 7 of the Constitution, instrumentalities of the Federal Government (such as the Customs Department) and instrumentalities of the Provincial Government (such as MRAs) both qualify as the State. It is a settled principle that a presumption of truth and correctness attaches to acts of State authorities. Consequently, a citizen, in discharging his onus of proof to establish that he/she is the lawful owner of a vehicle can rely on the registration issued by the MRA.

109. Section 25 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance details the manner in which the registration of a vehicle is to be made. Section 25(2) provides that a certificate of registration is to be issued to the owner of the vehicle. In other words, no person other than the owner of the vehicle can have a vehicle registered. Section 27 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance requires the owner of the vehicle to produce the same before the MRA at the time of registration. Section 28 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance provides grounds for refusal of registration, which include, inter alia, that the owner/applicant fails to produce import documents of the vehicle (in case of first-time registration) or the previous registration documents of the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 75 vehicle (in case of transfer of an already registered vehicle). The prescribed application form for registration of a vehicle includes the name of the owner and his credentials together with the particulars of the vehicle, including its chassis number, engine number and the year of manufacture, among other details. The certificate of registration (Form G), prescribed under sections 25(2) and 41(2) of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, records the name of the owner as well as the particulars of the vehicle.

110. The provisions of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance comprise a regulatory framework enabling the State to exercise oversight over vehicles. These provisions require that any change in the address of the owner be communicated to the MRA and that the vehicle be re-registered if it is used in another province for a period exceeding the prescribed duration. Section 33 requires that where a vehicle is altered in such manner that the particulars reflected in the certificate of registration, are no longer accurate, the owner must report such alteration to the MRA, which may then issue an amended certificate of registration, if necessary. Sections 34 and 35 provide for suspension and cancellation of registration in the event that the owner has furnished false statements or incorrect particulars as part of the application for registration of the vehicle.

111. In exercise of the authority under Section 43 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, the Islamabad Capital Territory (Seizure and Disposal of Motor Vehicles) Rules, 2014 (“Seizure and Disposal Rules”) have been promulgated. Rule 3 of the Seizure and Disposal Rules provides that a vehicle, whose registration certificate has been cancelled, or in relation to which the keeper of the vehicle fails to produce valid ownership documents, may Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 76 be taken into possession by the Excise and Taxation Officer. Rule 5(3) prescribes the issuance of notice to the owner of the vehicle requiring him to establish that he/she is a bona fide owner of the vehicle. Rule 7, which provides for confiscation of vehicles, stipulates that such consequence only flows in a case where a claimant is unable to prove his bona fide ownership of the vehicle. In other words, within the regulatory framework provided in terms of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance read with the Seizure and Disposal Rules, bona fide ownership of a vehicle is recognized as a defence against the penalty of confiscation by the MRA.

112. The scheme of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, particularly Chapter III that deals with registration of vehicles, provides for a title-based system for motor vehicles. The statute mandates that vehicles must be registered and prohibits their use without such registration. The regulatory framework prescribes the manner of registration, which includes scrutiny of the title of the owner through verification of import permits and/or purchase documents of the vehicle and scrutiny of the vehicle itself by verifying its particulars, including the year of manufacture, engine number, and chassis number etc. A certificate of registration is issued following such scrutiny and constitutes a title document that certifies the title of the owner, in whose name the vehicle is registered, as well as the particulars of the vehicle inscribed on the certificate of registration. Such document establishes that the registered owner is the bona fide owner of the vehicle whose particulars are reflected on the certificate of registration/registration card. In order to establish that the registered owner is not the bona fide owner of the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 77 vehicle, or that the particulars reflected in the certificate of registration are not the particulars of the vehicle in question but some other vehicle, it is for the Customs Department to dislodge the presumption of truth regarding ownership and particulars of the vehicle inscribed on the certificate of registration issued by the MRA. It simply cannot be that one arm of the State i.e. the Customs Department, is allowed to contest or deny a title document issued by another arm of the State i.e. the MRA, without rebutting the presumption of correctness on the basis of evidence adduced to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the vehicle in possession of the registered owner of the vehicle is not the one whose particulars are mentioned in the certificate of registration. The certificate of registration issued by the MRA therefore works as a representation by the State re the title of the vehicle as well as its particulars, the benefit of which goes to the owner. It is thus that for purposes of establishing a prima facie case that the person in possession of the vehicle is the bona fide owner of the vehicle, it is sufficient to prove a valid registration certificate/registration card. The Customs Department cannot be allowed to disregard the registration certificate as a title document because the State owes a fiduciary duty to its citizens. The State is a trustee of public power and must exercise its police and revenue-collection powers for the benefit of citizens. The duty that the State owes to a citizen includes the duty to protect the fundamental rights of citizens, as well as putting in place effective regulatory frameworks to prevent citizens from being harmed by illegal activities, without such frameworks becoming traps for innocent citizens. The State has a duty to act reasonably, which in terms of exercise of authority as part of public administration, includes the duty of Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 78 care and diligence. This duty is attracted where a vehicle is imported and cleared after scrutiny by Customs officials, where non-duty-paid or confiscated vehicles are auctioned by the State under any amnesty scheme or otherwise, and where the State verifies the particulars of the owner and the vehicle before issuing a registration certificate. Having assumed regulatory authority and having exercised it, whether as part of the customs clearance process, or as part of the vehicle registration process, the State cannot deny that a citizen is entitled to rely on the efficacy of the regulatory process and that the citizen cannot be burdened with the consequences of any negligence by the State as part of such process. If the State fails to exercise due care and diligence at the time of customs clearance or registration of a vehicle, a subsequent bona fide purchaser cannot be arbitrarily penalized for the State's prior negligence.

113. The proposition that the law must not be employed such that it functions as a trap for the citizen is conceptualized by the doctrine of legal certainty and rule of law. These doctrines dictate that the law must be clear, predictable and accessible so that a person of ordinary intelligence can understand what is required of him/her and can foresee and manage the legal consequences of his/her actions. The principle of individual autonomy (i.e. that the law respects citizens as rational beings capable of making choices), and the fault requirement as a precondition for imposing penal sanction, form part of the notion of rule of law. It is in this context that the claim of a bona fide owner of a vehicle, who has not been proven culpable by virtue of either knowing or reasonably suspecting that a vehicle is smuggled, cannot be disregarded while deciding whether such Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 79 owner or his property is liable for an offence in terms of clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act.

114. While the Supreme Court in Abdul Karim has drawn a distinction between the concept of ―lawful authority‖ used in Section 187 and ―lawful excuse‖ used in clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act, it bears mention here that the owner of a registered vehicle who is able to establish his title in relation to such property by virtue of a registration certificate issued by the MRA discharges the prima facie onus to establish lawful authority to possess such vehicle. Where such owner further establishes that he purchased such vehicle for full market value, which he can establish through banking transactions, such owner also discharges the prima facie burden of proof to establish that the vehicle cannot be regarded as the proceeds of crime in terms of the first proviso to Section 187 of the Customs Act. In such circumstances, it then falls on the Customs Department to prove on a balance of probability through relevant material that the presumptions in favor of the owner of the vehicle stand rebutted on the basis of evidence that either the owner had knowledge or reasonable basis to suspect that the vehicle was smuggled, or because the particulars of the vehicle claimed by the owner, as reflected in the registration book, relate to another vehicle that has been identified and/or traced by the Customs authorities. How the legal onus stands discharged by the Customs Department on a balance of probabilities will obviously depend on the facts and circumstances of each case and no objective test can be laid down in such regard.

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 80 115. We have taken cognizance of the larger constitutional context within which provisions of the Customs Act generally and the offences and penalties prescribed under Section 156 of the Customs Act more particularly are to be understood. Let us now consider the case law that has evolved in relation to application of penalties under the Customs Act, while identifying infirmities in the proceedings leading up to the application of penalties rendering the penalty of confiscation of property unsustainable in the eyes of law. We will consider the case law in accordance with the various stages in an adjudicatory proceeding leading up to imposition of penalty and use of confiscated property sequentially. After having considered such law, we will analyze certain issues that continue to arise in relation to imposition of penalties under clauses (9), (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act, including, inter alia, the question of wrongdoing on the basis of which a penalty can be imposed, the question of attribution of bonafides to an owner as a defence against imposition of penalty and the question of use and disposal of confiscated property under various CGOs issued by the FBR.

The Show-Cause Notice and due process requirements 116. It was held by the Supreme Court in The Collector Central Excise and the Land Customs and others vs. Rahm Din (1987 SCMR 1840) that, “section 180 of the Act requires that no order for confiscation of any goods, can be passed, unless the owner of the goods is informed in writing (or if the person concerned consents in writing, then orally) of the grounds on which it was proposed to confiscate the goods. The section also makes a mandatory provision for giving an opportunity of Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 81 being heard to the affected person. On a plain reading of the provisions of section 180, it is fairly plain that the grounds on which the Customs Authorities proposed to confiscate the goods must state precisely and clearly the facts which constitute the customs offence. Therefore the requirements of reasonable opportunity of being heard would be satisfied only when the particulars of the facts alleged and grounds are brought to the notice of the person proceeded against and the order of confiscation is fully passed upon such grounds.” In the said case, the Show-Cause Notice asserted that an individual had failed to make a declaration with regard to foreign currency in his possession when asked by the Customs Staff to do so. The imposition of penalty was however based on the finding that the individual had brought foreign currency into the country through an unauthorized route constituting the offence of smuggling in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act. In such circumstances, the confiscation order based on a ground not mentioned in the Show-Cause Notice was held to be palpably illegal.

117. It was explained by Division Bench of the Lahore High Court in Caretex vs. Collector Sales Tax and Federal Excise and others (2013 PTD 1536) that, “Show-Cause Notice, is a foundational document, which is to comprehensively describe the case made out against the taxpayer by making reference to the evidence collected in support of the same. It is the narration of facts in the Show Cause Notice along with the supporting evidence which determines the offense attracted in a particular case. Show Cause Notice is not a casual correspondence or a tool or license to commence a roving inquiry into the affairs of the taxpayer based on assumptions and speculations but is a Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 82 fundamental document that carries definitive legal and factual position of the department against the taxpayer.”

118. In Muhammad Riaz vs. Collector of Customs (2020 PTD 2197), it was alleged by the Customs Department that the chassis number of the vehicle was tampered/self-punched. In this matter, the Lahore High Court found that the Show-Cause Notice had not been issued within two months of the seizure. Consequently, the vehicle was ordered to be released and for determination of the question of smuggling on the factual side, the vehicle was remanded back to the Tribunal.
119. It was affirmed by the Supreme Court in Commissioner Inland Revenue, Chenab Zone, RTO, Faisalabad vs. Messrs Rose Food Industries, Faisalabad and another (2023 SCMR 2070) that:

“The principles of fairness and due process are an integral part of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 10A of the Constitution. It guarantees that every person is entitled to a fair trial and due process for determination of rights and obligations. The issuance of a show cause notice is the most crucial in the context of a fair trial and due process. It enables a taxpayer to precisely know what allegations are to be met, explained and answered to the satisfaction of the adjudication officer. It is the duty of the Department to ensure that a show cause notice is issued after a proper inquiry and investigation. It should be manifest from the contents of the show cause notice that it was issued after ascertaining the facts and the allegations are not vague or ambiguous. The charges or allegations should be specific, otherwise the taxpayer would be prejudiced and denied the right to a fair trial. As a corollary, the adjudication authority has to confine the proceedings to the specific charges and allegations clearly mentioned in the show cause notice and cannot Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 83 adjudicate any charge or allegation beyond it.
Adjudicating a charge or allegation not confronted in the show cause notice would not be sustainable in law.”

120. It is well settled, as is manifest from the case law cited above, that a Show-Cause Notice must put to the individual threatened with the imposition of a penalty, the precise case against him in order for him to discharge his onus to establish in terms of Section 187 of the Customs Act read with relevant provisions of Section 156 of the Customs Act that he is not liable for the penalty proposed to be inflicted on him. The adjudicatory proceedings are therefore confined to the charge as articulated within the Show-Cause Notice. To comply with requirements of Article 10A of the Constitution, neither can adjudicatory proceedings be broadened beyond the scope of the Show-Cause Notice nor can a penalty be imposed on a basis different from one that naturally flows from the content of the Show-Cause Notice.

Seizure cannot be made on the basis of suspicion 121. Section 168 of the Customs Act vests in officers of the Customs Department the discretionary authority to seize any goods liable to confiscation. Section 168(1) of the Customs Act further provides that when not practicable to seize any such goods, the officer “may serve on the owner of the goods or any person holding them in his possession or charge and order that he shall not remove, part with, or otherwise deal with the goods except with the previous permission of such officer.” The plain language of Section 168 of the Customs Act clearly provides that the authority created by it is discretionary in nature and must be exercised bearing in mind the constitutional framework, which vests in citizens the right to liberty and the right to hold their Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 84 property in terms of Article 9 and 23 of the Constitution. Such discretionary authority must therefore be exercised in a manner that is least restrictive to the rights of an individual pending adjudication of whether or not the property in question is liable to be confiscated.

122. Where property is indeed seized in exercise of authority under Section 168 of the Customs Act, Section 169 of the Customs Act provides how it must be dealt with: it must be delivered into the care of a customs officer or be deposited at a customs house nearest to the place of seizure. Section 169(4) of the Customs Act provides that property seized may be sold in accordance with provisions of Section 201 even during the pendency of adjudicatory proceedings. The scope of such power and the manner of its exercise will be dealt with later in this judgment when we consider the matter of disposal of confiscated goods.

123. It bears mention that the FBR has issued detailed instructions in exercise of authority under Section 223 of the Customs Act prescribing the steps to be taken for the storage of seized/confiscated goods in the State warehouses. These instructions in Chapter-IX of the CGOs appear to be in conflict with CGOs issued to make allowance for the use and disposal of confiscated vehicles. The legality of CGOs providing for use and disposal of confiscated vehicles will also be discussed later in this judgment.

124. For our present purpose, it would suffice to re-emphasize that it was held by the Supreme Court in Collector Customs, Sales Tax and Central Excise vs. Professor Muhammad Khan (2007 SCMR 10) that vehicles cannot be detained and Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 85 seized on grounds of suspicion alone. In the said matter, a vehicle was detained even after the owner showed documents of registration of the vehicle, which was registered in his name. The vehicle was however detained for failure to produce import documents. The Supreme Court held that the Customs authorities were not vested with unbridled powers under provisions of the Customs Act “to detain the goods of foreign origin at any time by raising the presumption that the same were not brought into Pakistan in a lawful manner. The Customs Authorities and such other public functionaries are not above the law to command absolute authority in exercise of their power and in the absence of any proof that goods in possession of a person were brought into Pakistan in violation of any law, have no authority to detain such goods merely on the basis of suspicion.” The Supreme Court went on to note that the detention of the vehicle in such circumstances was an act of high handedness that rendered the officials concerned liable to be proceeded against for misconduct in terms of the Civil Servants (E&D) Rules, 1973, read with Removal from Service (Special Powers) Ordinance, 2000. The matter was referred to Chairman FBR for further action.

Relevance of the Chain of Custody 125. The principle that case property must remain in safe custody, starting with the recovery of such property and continuing through trial/adjudicatory proceedings, is a well settled proposition. Where characteristics of property are being relied on by the State to prove a case against an accused, such property forms an essential link in the evidentiary chain and any break in this chain creates doubt about the State's case, the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 86 benefit of which goes to the accused [see for example Wahid Bux alias Wahido vs. The State (2022 Pcr. LJ 1631), Muhammad Ahsan Kamal and others vs. The State (2020 Pcr. LJ (Note) 12), and Muhammad Shakeel alias Banarsi vs. The State (2021 Pcr. LJ 1887)].

126. The importance of chain of custody has been highlighted in the case law that has developed in relation to provisions of the Control of Narcotics Substances Act, 1997. In The State through Regional Director ANF vs. Imam Bakhsh (2018 SCMR 2039), the Supreme Court held that the chain of custody of samples of the seized drug and its dispatch to the narcotics testing laboratory, “is pivotal, as the entire construct of the Act and the Rules rests on the Report of the Government Analyst, which in turn rests on the process of sampling and its safe and secure custody and transmission to the laboratory. The prosecution must establish that the chain of custody was unbroken, unsuspicious, indubitable, safe and secure. Any break in the chain of custody or lapse in the control of possession of the sample, will cast doubts on the safe custody and safe transmission of the sample(s) and will impair and vitiate the conclusiveness and reliability of the Report of the Government Analyst, thus, rendering it incapable of sustaining conviction.” The Supreme Court went on to hold that the report of the Government Analyst must follow internationally recognized protocols, without which such report would have no sanctity.

127. It was once again held by the Supreme Court in Zahir Shah alias Shat vs. The State (2019 SCMR 2004) that, “this court has repeatedly held that safe and safe transmission of the drug from the spot of recovery till its receipt by the Narcotics Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 87 Testing Laboratory must be satisfactorily established. This chain of custody is fundamental as the report of the Government Analyst is the main evidence for the purpose of conviction. The prosecution must establish that chain of custody was unbroken, unsuspicious, safe and secure. Any break in the chain of custody i.e., safe custody or safe transmission impairs and vitiates the conclusiveness and reliability of the Report of the Government Analyst, thus, rendering it incapable of sustaining conviction.”

128. It was held by a Division Branch of the Sindh High Court in The Collector of Customs and others vs. Zeeshan and others (2022 PTD 1330), in relation to a case involving a vehicle that allegedly had a tampered Vehicle Identification Number (“VIN”), that, “goods under examination are sent out to third party’s examination, the chain of safe custody is broken and examination reports coming from an alien department (to the controversy) would always be shrouded in doubts and be considered with a pinch of salt. In usual legal processes, such an evidence or incriminating material is not to be relied upon unless the test is conducted in the presence of the affected party (i.e. the importer in the case at hand), such an outcome also vitiates Article 10-A of the Constitution which provides for transparency and fair trial.”

129. The principle laid down with regard to safe custody of case property and safe transmission of property to a laboratory in circumstances where the laboratory report is a pivotal piece of evidence relied upon by the State to establish wrongdoing and impose penalty, as highlighted in relation to CNSA offences, are applicable to the allegation of wrongdoing and liability for owning and/or possessing a vehicle alleged to be smuggled on the basis Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 88 that such vehicle has a tampered chassis number. In such cases, the pivotal piece of evidence on the basis of which it is presumed that the vehicle is smuggled is that its chassis number is tampered. The allegation of tampering of the chassis number is then backed by a Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report. Where the vehicle has not retained in safe custody starting with its detention and/or seizure, and the vehicle has not been subjected to examination for purposes of producing the FSL report in the presence of the vehicle owner, the state will be unable to establish safe custody of the vehicle and its safe transmission for purposes of producing an FSL report. This, in turn, raises questions about the reliability of the evidence on the basis of which liability is being attributed to the vehicle owner, resulting in confiscation of such vehicle. In view of Article 187A read with Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, an FSL report stating that the vehicle has a tampered chassis number is often used as the only evidence to establish that the vehicle is smuggled. However, examination of the vehicle leading to an FSL report is mostly undertaken days or weeks after the vehicle has been detained and seized by Customs authorities, without the vehicle being detained in a customs warehouse such that its safe custody and lack of access to irrelevant individuals can be established. Further, the examination of the vehicle is often undertaken without associating the owner of the vehicle with the process. This raises doubts about when the chassis number was tampered and who was responsible for such tampering. In the cases before us, the Customs Department has liberally exercised its power to seize in terms of Section 168 of the Customs Act and has not followed protocols for safe custody of vehicles in terms of Section 169 of the Customs Act, raising questions about Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 89 whether the tampering of the chassis number took place while the vehicle was in the possession of the owner of such vehicle, or thereafter once it was in the possession of the Customs Department. The use of seized vehicles by the Customs Department has been flagged by superior Courts repeatedly, without the Customs Department and the FBR paying heed and taking corrective steps.

130. In the matter of Muhammad Farooq vs. Muhammad Mubeen Akhtar and 7 others (2004 Pcr. LJ 1958), the Lahore High Court was seized of a case, wherein buses made by Hino Pak were seized by the Customs Department on the basis of an FSL report that the chassis number was fake. While holding that the seizure was not sustainable in terms of Section 171 of the Customs Act, the Customs Department had failed to produce any evidence of smuggling, and that the FSL report in itself was insufficient, the Lahore High Court issued a general direction stating that, “the Forensic Science Laboratory will submit a report after examining the vehicle in the presences of the concerned person/party and ex parte report would not be accepted.”

131. In Collector of Customs, Peshawar vs. Saleh Jan (Civil Appeal No.58-P of 2010), the matter before the Supreme Court related to a vehicle, the chassis number of which had been tampered with. It was revealed during the adjudicatory proceedings before the Tribunal that the chassis number as deciphered from the first FSL report was different from that reported by the second FSL report. The Customs authorities explained that the vehicle had remained in use by Customs authorities and had met a serious accident due to which the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 90 chassis number had been totally defaced. The Supreme Court noted that, “it appears that some tampering was done to the chassis number of the vehicle as a result of which it became defaced and this perhaps happened when the vehicle was in the use of the Customs authorities.” The Supreme Court found that this created doubt, the benefit of which would go to the owner of the vehicle, especially in circumstances where the Customs authorities had not carried out any investigation and diligence in relation to the entire record related to the vehicle, including the record available with Port authorities as well as MRA.

132. This Court in Collector of Customs, Model Customs Collectorate (MCC), Islamabad vs. M/s. Aurangzeb and 2 others (Customs Reference No.20 of 2020) in its judgment dated 21.02.2022, while upholding the order of the Tribunal noting that the Customs Department had failed to discharge the onus that the vehicle was smuggled in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, held that, “the report of the Forensic Science Laboratory obtained without associating the respondents was definitely not sufficient to establish commission of the offence under Section 2(s).”

133. To the extent that attribution of liability and imposition of penalty under clauses (9), (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act entail a fault-element, it is imperative that the evidence produced to discharge the legal burden establishing fault/wrongdoing and providing the justification for imposition of penalty should be such that is safe and reliable. Where the allegation is that the chassis number of a vehicle has been tampered to obfuscate its identity, either because it has been brought in through an unauthorized route or that duties and Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 91 taxes have otherwise not been paid in relation to it and its chassis number has been tampered or altered to match the chassis number of another lawfully imported vehicle, it is imperative that the safe custody of the vehicle and its safe transmission for purposes of generating an FSL report is established through record. And further that the report of the FSL is issued after following standard protocols such that its finding can be treated as a reliable with regard to the identity and particulars of the vehicle. It is important to note that as a safety feature, as well as due to regulatory requirements across various jurisdictions, manufacturers of vehicles inscribe the VIN at multiple places in a vehicle. The chassis number is one such VIN. The VINs are also often inscribed on the pillar of the door and in other hidden places so that if the VIN in one place is defaced the other VINs inscribed on the vehicle and its parts can be used to determine the true identity of the vehicle.

134. During the proceedings that form the subject-matter of the references before us, we have not seen an FSL report or any other material produced by Customs authorities that seeks to determine the identity of the vehicle based on tracing the VINs inscribed at various places in the vehicles in question, even in relation to models produced over the last decade where the practice of inscribing VINs in multiple places in vehicles has become a standard practice with vehicle manufacturers. In a case where the chassis number (i.e. the VIN number stamped on the vehicle frame) is found to be tampered, the other VIN numbers (often stamped or printed on the dashboard, door jamb, under the seat or spare tire etc.) can be located to determine if they match with one another and the particulars of Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 92 the vehicle as mentioned in the import/registration documents to verify the identity of the vehicle with some certainty. No such inquiry was undertaken by the Customs Departments in any of the cases before us.

The standard of proof and the onus of proof 135. There appears to have been some confusion created due to conflicting case law as to whether an FSL report stating that the chassis number of a vehicle is tampered is sufficient proof to attract the penalty of confiscation of a vehicle. The associated question of relevance is what material or evidence must the Customs Department produce to bring home the charge that a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is to be regarded as a smuggled vehicle on the balance of probabilities. In this regard, we will first consider the cases relied on by the Customs Department in support of confiscation on the basis that the chassis number is tampered, followed by cases where it has been held that the FSL report or the fact that the chassis number of a vehicle is tampered is not dispositive of the question of whether the vehicle is in fact smuggled.

136. In Ch. Maqbool Ahmed, the case before a two-member Bench of the Supreme Court related to a vehicle with a cut and weld chassis plate, the confiscation of which was ordered in terms of Section 156(1)(89) of the Customs Act. The Supreme Court took into account the fact that the vehicle according to its registration book was a 1987 model Mitsubishi Pajero. Its physical verification however established that it was a 1991 model Mitsubishi Pajero. The Supreme Court held that the particulars entered in the registration book related to another vehicle and turned down the request that the vehicle be released Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 93 subject to payment of duty. The Supreme Court also rejected the request for cross-examination of the FSL expert on the basis that there were three FSL reports on record establishing that the chassis plate was cut and weld and that presumption of truth attached to such FSL reports.

137. The second most cited case in support of confiscation of vehicles with tampered chassis numbers is Sultan Muhammad. The Peshawar High Court in the said matter summarized applicable principles of law after reviewing existing case law. It was held by the Peshawar High Court that a presumption of truth attached to FSL reports being official acts, but that in case of serious infirmities appearing on the record evidence of the official who carried out the forensic examination could be recorded. However, “in case repeated forensic examinations confirm tampering of the chassis number of the vehicle, then there is no requirement for the maker of the report to be summoned and cross-examined by the owner.” Tampering of the chassis number was defined to include, “any alteration of the original chassis number of the vehicle, whether manual or otherwise or cutting a piece of the frame and re-welding another piece thereon or chassis number filled with welding material and then re-stamped.” The Peshawar High Court further held that, “tampering of chassis number as a result of an accident of the vehicle could only be a valid ground, if the same was reported to and confirmed by the Motor Vehicle Authorities under Section 33 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965,” and that, “public auction of vehicles having tampered chassis numbers have been prohibited and are liable to be confiscated.” The Peshawar High Court also found that, confiscated vehicles having tampered Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 94 chassis numbers are only allowed for use by Government Departments on payment of nominal/token prices in view of Customs Circular No.10(1)AS/2004 dated 11.12.2007. The Peshawar High Court took into account the judgment of the Supreme Court in Federation of Pakistan through Director- General of Intelligence and Investigation-FBR, Karachi vs. Muhammad Jamal Rizvi and others (2012 SCMR 169) and other cases where Customs authorities had continued to use detained vehicles and held that, “even a positive FSL report of a vehicle in use of the Customs authorities would create a doubt on the presumption of truth attached to the said report that the tampering took place when the vehicle was being used by the Customs authorities.”

138. The judgment of the Peshawar High Court was relied upon by a three-member Bench of the Supreme Court in Sarfraz Khan. While relying on the definition of tampering provided in Sultan Muhammad, the Supreme Court held that, “presenting documentation, relating to the said tampered vehicle from the Motor Vehicle Authority, without specific approval for the alteration in the chassis or engine number, as envisaged under Section 33 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965, would be of no legal avail.” In the said matter, the vehicle owner conceded that some alteration had been made to the vehicle, but that such alteration had been made by the person from whom the vehicle was purchased. The Supreme Court disregarded such explanation and held that if the owner had purchased the vehicle, “without taking due care and complying with the requirements of law, he cannot claim to be a bonafide purchaser. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 95 Needless to say that he may, if so advised, claim damages from the person from whom he purchased the subject vehicle.”

139. The Lahore High Court in Collector of Customs, Multan vs. Muhammad Tasleem (2002 MLD 296) endorsed observations of the Tribunal rendered in the matter holding that the principle of bonafide purchaser in good faith and without notice was not applicable when it came to goods confiscated under provisions of the Customs Act. This same observation was repeated in Aman Ullah vs. Customs, Central Excise and Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Lahore and 4 others (2007 PTD 983) in the context of liability to pay customs duties, taxes and fine, while holding that even a bonafide purchaser for consideration could not be absolved of the duty to pay duties and taxes in relation to the goods owned by such purchaser.

140. It is well understood that not every vehicle with a tampered chassis number falls within the domain of Customs authorities for purposes of enforcement of provisions of the Customs Act. For example, vehicles that are either not found to be smuggled or in relation to which there is no allegation that taxes and duties at the time of import were not paid fall beyond the scope of the Customs Act. Similarly, locally manufactured vehicles, even those with tampered chassis numbers, do not attract provisions of the Customs Act. With this clarification, let us now consider the case law highlighting infirmities in adjudicatory proceedings resulting in imposition of the penalty of confiscation of a vehicle.

141. It was held by the Lahore High Court in Commercial Union Insurance Company vs. Collector, Customs (1994 MLD 2154) that, “the registration of a stolen vehicle on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 96 basis of fake document not involving any tax liability is a matter to be resolved on the basis of title by the Court having jurisdiction and not by the customs people. The function of the authorities under Customs Act, 1969, is to decide the matter of leviable taxes and in case it is found that an item was smuggled, an appropriate order including confiscation of the property can be passed under the relevant provisions of law. The mere finding that the goods to have been initially brought into the country against a prohibition or restriction in the absence of any proof through an enquiry regarding the payment of customs duty is not sufficient to pass the order of confiscation.” It was reiterated by the Peshawar High Court in Sultan Muhammad that, “locally manufactured vehicles are beyond the legal mandate of the Revenue under the Act.”

142. Logically speaking, it is not just imported vehicles whose chassis numbers can be tampered with. Locally manufactured vehicles and vehicles lawfully imported into Pakistan and released by Customs authorities after payment of taxes and duties are equally vulnerable to having their chassis numbers tampered. The literature on the phenomenon of tampering establishes that stolen vehicles are susceptible to having their chassis numbers tampered. The object of such exercise is to clone the identity of a stolen vehicle to transform it into another legally registered vehicle. The cloned identity then includes the tampered VIN, registration documents and fake license plates. The second object of tampering chassis numbers is to prepare them for use in illicit activities such that their identities are untraceable, so that the vehicles cannot be linked back to the perpetrators of crime. In many jurisdictions vehicles that are Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 97 subjected to a major accident after which they are deemed by the insurance company to be a total loss, vehicles can be illegally rebuilt to obfuscate the accident history. In such cases too, the VIN is tampered to hide the reconstruction of the vehicle, which raises concerns about the safety of the vehicle for driving purposes. The point is that tampering with the identity of a smuggled vehicle is not the only incidence of tampering. It is only where a chassis number has been tampered in order to clone its identity and hide the fact that it is either smuggled or has been illegally imported and released without payment of taxes and duties that Customs authorities acquire a role under provisions of the Customs Act.

143. In the matter of Collector of Customs and another vs. Zeeshan Iftikhar (Civil Petition No.1217 of 2003) an appeal came before the Supreme Court against a judgment of the Division Bench of the Peshawar High Court that involved a vehicle that had been detained on the charge of having been smuggled. But the vehicle was subsequently forfeited on the basis that the parts installed in the vehicle were smuggled. The Peshawar High Court ordered the release of the vehicle, which was upheld by the Supreme Court, while noting that, “no investigation was conducted to ascertain as to whether accessories allegedly changed by the owner of the vehicle were custom paid or otherwise.” And that in such circumstances without the Customs authorities discharging their onus of proof to establish that the parts installed were smuggled the vehicle could not have been confiscated.

144. In the matter of Collector of Customs, Peshawar vs. Fahim Khan and another (Civil Petition No. 117 of 2006) Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 98 an appeal came before the Supreme Court against an order passed by the Peshawar High Court, wherein the Peshawar High Court had held that, “where Customs authorities had no evidence that the vehicle in question was smuggled in/imported into Pakistan without payment of leviable duties and where to the contrary bill of entry was confirmed, mere fact that chassis number was refitted and in absence of any evidence that with such chassis number some other vehicle is plying, the seizure, forfeiture/confiscation of the vehicle would thus be beyond the jurisdiction of Customs authorities.” These observations were reproduced and endorsed by the Supreme Court.

145. The Peshawar High Court once again in Sudeer vs. Collector Customs, Peshawar and 2 others (2010 PTD 1333) reiterated that the tampering of a chassis number without additional evidence establishing that the vehicle in question was not one that was legally imported and in relation to which duties and taxes were paid, the vehicle was not liable for confiscation.

146. In Raja Sahadat Nawaz vs. Superintendent of Police (2003 YLR 1431), the Lahore High Court was seized of a matter seeking quashment of the FIR in a case involving a vehicle with a tampered chassis number. The Lahore High Court held that the FSL report was antedated and maneuvered and that where no fraud or forgery was established and there was no rival claimant or owner of the vehicle, the petitioner had successfully proved that he was a bonafide purchaser.

147. In Collector of Customs vs. Hilal Muhammad (2003 PTD 562), the case involved a Toyota Hiace with a cut and weld chassis plate. The Court took into account that the chassis plate Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 99 had rusted and three of its sides were welded and that the Federal Investigation Report and the FSL report were in conflict. It concluded that there was no evidence establishing that the vehicle was imported in an unauthorized manner or through an unauthorized route, which was then ordered to be released.

148. In Muhammad Aslam Azad vs. Collector of Customs (2005 PTD 1949), the Lahore High Court dealt with the matter involving a 1991 model Toyota Land Cruiser, registered in 1996, that had been confiscated for having a refitted chassis plate. The Lahore High Court noted that merely by virtue of the last four digits of the chassis number not being deciphered according to the FSL report, “the appellant could not be saddled with mens rea that he smuggled the vehicle of which all other particulars resemble with the vehicle imported… Furthermore, there is also no evidence that chassis plate was tampered with by the applicant.” In such circumstances, benefit of doubt was given to the bonafide purchaser.

149. In Haji Rab Nawaz vs. The State (2009 Pcr. LJ 945), the allegation against the owner was that the chassis number was tampered and the registration book was bogus. The Peshawar High Court noted that there was no rival claimant of the vehicle and it had not been established that the vehicle was stolen. It was held that only because the chassis number was tampered the, “vehicle cannot be confiscated to the State because under West Pakistan Motor Vehicles Ordinance, 1965, 1965, at the most, such vehicle cannot be driven on the road under Section 23 of the ordinance.” It was directed that the vehicle be released after registration under Section 25 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance and entry of alterations by the Motor Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 100 Registration Authority in terms of Section 33 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance.

150. In Manzoor Ahmad and another vs. Customs Appellate Tribunal, Islamabad Bench, etc. (Custom Reference No.41 of 2015), the Peshawar High Court in judgment dated 13.04.2022 held that, “there is no force in the contention raised by the learned counsel for the Department that since the Laboratory had confirmed the chassis to be cut and weld, therefore, the factum of the vehicle being smuggled stood established. This argument is misconceived because confirmation of the chassis being cut and weld is not the sole and conclusive factor to establish that the vehicle was smuggled. The vehicle was registered long ago and the likelihood of damage on account of accident cannot be ruled out. However, in the case in hand, we are satisfied that a reasonable opportunity ought to be extended to the applicants to controvert the prosecution case on the factual side. The principles of procedural fairness are embedded in Article 10-A of the Constitution and their observance is mandatory.” The matter was then remanded back to the Tribunal.

151. Let us now consider the manner in which property is to be preserved during the pendency of the adjudicatory process, in the context of the power vested in Customs authorities under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act to “cause the thing [liable to confiscation seized under Section 168] to be sold in accordance with the provisions of section 201 and have the proceeds kept in deposit pending adjudication of the case or as the case may be, disposal of the appeal or the final judgment by the Court.” Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 101 152. The first thing to note about this provision is that it is a discretionary power that is to be exercised in a just, fair and reasonable manner while preserving the requirements of due process during the adjudicatory proceedings. While this provision applies across the board to any and all goods seized by Customs authorities under Section 168 of the Customs Act, there are considerations that are to be borne in mind when such discretion is exercised in relation to vehicles that are alleged to be smuggled, as has been touched upon earlier in this judgment while discussing the need for safe custody of case property and safe transmission in undertaking examination of the vehicle for purposes of producing FSL reports. The first such special consideration to note is that a vehicle is not a property subject to speedy or natural decay. And as has been held in the earlier part of this judgment, as the primary evidence in support of the Customs case that a tampered vehicle is a smuggled vehicle, is the tampered chassis plate (in the category of cases that we are dealing with), it is imperative to preserve the vehicle as case property alongwith the tampered chassis plate on which is founded the claim of the Customs Department that the vehicle be regarded as smuggled. The confiscation of a vehicle can be ordered by Collector Customs, who, while empowered to exercise adjudicatory authority, falls within the hierarchy of the Customs Department. It is the Tribunal that is regarded as the last fact finding forum within the adjudicatory hierarchy, and consequently the case property (in this case the vehicle itself) ought not be disposed of in discharge of the discretionary authority vested in Customs officials under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act until a definitive factual determination has been rendered by the Tribunal after appraising the relevant Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 102 evidence/material on which the case of the Customs Department is built.

153. The second point to note is that Section 201(2) prescribes the manner in which sale proceeds are to be applied, and includes, inter alia, that such proceeds are to be applied to pay customs duty, and other taxes and dues payable to the Federal Government in respect of the goods in question. The question of whether a vehicle is smuggled and/or whether or not taxes and duties have been paid in relation thereto, is a matter that is to be determined upon conclusion of the adjudicatory proceedings. Consequently, the purpose of providing this extraordinary discretionary authority to sell a seized good liable to confiscation pending adjudication of the matter (i.e. to cater to situations where the goods in question may lose value when susceptible to natural decay or otherwise may frustrate the interest of the State in disposing of the goods to recover taxes and duties due to the Government), are not attracted in a case involving a seized vehicle suspected of being smuggled. On the contrary, in the case of a fire sale undertaken under provisions of Section 169(4) read with Section 201 of the Customs Act, the value received in such auction proceedings is expected to be less than the fair market value of such vehicle. In the event that at the conclusion of adjudicatory proceedings, the conclusion drawn by the Court is that the vehicle is not smuggled and/or liable to confiscation, the effect of premature sales/disposal of such vehicle would be that of exposing the State and public revenue to a claim of damages by the owner of the vehicle. Such exercise of discretionary authority under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act is therefore not just, fair and reasonable and falls foul of the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 103 requirements of Section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (“General Clauses Act”).

154. The third consideration re disposal of a vehicle pending adjudication is of a constitutional nature. Article 10-A guarantees the right of a citizen to due process and fair trial in adjudication of his/her civil rights and liabilities. Such adjudicatory process must be structured in consonance with Article 175 of the Constitution that provides for separation of powers. The principle of separation of powers, for purposes of adjudicatory proceedings under the provisions of the Customs Act, is upheld by providing an appropriate remedy before the High Court in terms of Section 196 of the Customs Act. In a matter where on the basis of an order of seizure passed by Customs authorities, pending adjudication of the claim of the Customs Department, the vehicle in question is disposed of by the Customs Department in a manner that the fair market value of the vehicle has not been independently determined, resulting in a loss to the vehicle owner, who at the end of the adjudicatory proceedings stands vindicated in terms of his/her ownership of the property, the premature sales/disposal of the vehicle would amount to a confiscatory action in breach of the rights guaranteed by Article 24 read with Article 10-A of the Constitution. In order not to raise such constitutional concerns, it is imperative that the discretionary power vested in Customs authorities under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act to auction/dispose of a seized vehicle not be exercised till the adjudicatory proceedings have attained finality before the Tribunal or before the High Court, in the event that a reference is filed.

Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 104 155.
