A natural corollary of the above principle is that seized and/or confiscated vehicles must be preserved as case property till such time that the decision with regard to civil forfeiture and/or imposition of taxes and duties attains finality in terms of the adjudicatory remedies provided under the Customs Act all the way up to the High Court. In this context, let us consider Section 182 of the Customs Act, which provides that goods confiscated under the Customs Act shall vest in the Federal Government forthwith and that Customs officials shall take possession of such confiscated goods. The proviso to Section 182 of the Customs Act then provides that, “the Board may authorize the use of confiscated vehicles for operational purposes by the Board or, with the approval of the Board, its subordinate offices.” The principles enumerated in relation to disposal of vehicles in terms of Section 168(4) of the Customs Act squarely apply to the use of confiscated vehicles during the pendency of adjudicatory proceedings till such time that they have attained finality.

156. As has been emphasized in the earlier part of this judgment, Article 23 of the Constitution protects the right of a citizen to hold and enjoy his/her property. We have noted above in detail how any reasonable restrictions imposed in relation to the enjoyment of such right must constitute the least restrictive means to protect and promote legitimate State purpose. Section 182 of the Customs Act is to be read as contemplating goods the declaration of confiscation in relation to which has attained finality through the adjudicatory process. Any other reading would fall foul of the principles of separation of power as well as fair trial and due process already highlighted above. Section 182 Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 105 of the Customs Act cannot be read as an arbitrary power vested in Customs authorities or the FBR to commandeer property belonging to a citizen, the status and fate of which is yet to be adjudicated within the adjudicatory hierarchy provided under the Customs Act. It cannot be contemplated that the Legislature, while introducing Section 182 of the Customs Act, sought to vest in the Customs Department the right to compulsorily acquire the possession of a vehicle, constituting private property of a citizen, for enjoyment and use of public officials free of charge, without compensating the citizen of such acquisition of his/her property without compensation, in the event that it is ultimately determined by the Tribunal or the High Court that the vehicle did not constitute a smuggled good and was not liable to confiscation.

157. It is in the context of the proviso to Section 182 of the Customs Act that the legal sanctity of the CGOs issued for purposes of determining the use and/or disposal of confiscated vehicles is to be considered. In the earlier part of this judgment, we have already considered how delegated authority to enact subsidiary legislation and/or issue administrative instructions must be exercised within the four corners of the parent legislation to realize the objects of such legislation. From this perspective, it must be borne in mind that the limited authorization for use of confiscated vehicles in terms of the proviso to Section 182 of the Customs Act is limited to “operational purposes by the Board or, with approval of the Board, its subordinate offices.” We have already noted above that the time when such power of the FBR to authorize use of confiscated vehicles vests is once the adjudicatory remedies Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 106 stand exhausted, and the title of the vehicle definitively vests in the Federal Government.

158. The second point to note is that neither Section 182 nor any other provision of the Customs Act vests in either the Federal Government or the FBR the power to sell confiscated vehicles, that constitute State property, in a non-transparent manner to other Government departments on nominal rates. With this prelude, let us now consider the CGOs issued with regard to regulating the disposal of confiscated vehicles.

159. At the outset, it is important to note that such CGOs may be considered as instructions or directions issued in terms of Section 223 of the Customs Act, which provision does not vest in FBR the authority to issue subordinate legal instruments for purposes of disposing State property. CGOs are not rules framed in exercise of powers under Section 219 of the Customs Act.

160. The learned counsels for the Customs Department during the pendency of the proceedings relied on various CGOs to justify the disposal of confiscated vehicles to various Government Departments. We will consider the content of such CGOs before proceeding with the legal questions that arise in relation to them. The first CGO brought to the attention of this Court is an order issued by the FBR dated 11.12.2007, while relying on a decision of the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) dated 03.03.2006, re disposal of confiscated tampered vehicles. The ECC decision, as reflected in the CGO, states the following:

(i) Buses and vans may be utilized for pick and drop of officers and staff working in CBR headquarters and its field formations; Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 107 (ii) Other vehicles (cars, jeeps etc.) may be sold to the Government/semi-Government departments on the highest prices offered by them; and (iii) Any leftover vehicles may be offered free of cost to the Government owned educational, medical and scientific institutions, as recommended by the respective Ministries, on first come first served basis.

161. The Customs Department also placed on record SRO 568(I)/2008 dated 11.06.2008, which provided that smuggled vehicles other than ones with tempered engine or chassis numbers seized on or before 31.05.2008 could be released on payment of leviable duties and taxes in addition to redemption fine. The latest CGO relied on by the Customs Department is CGO No.05 of 2018 dated 24.05.2018 (“CGO No.05”). This CGO also relies on ECC decision dated 03.03.2006. In terms of eligibility it provides that, “Federal/Provincial Government/Semi- Government departments and Government owned educational, medical and scientific institutions” are eligible for purchase of tampered vehicles. Clause 3(3) of CGO No.05 then provides that the purchasing department is responsible for registration of the tampered vehicle in its own name with the relevant Motor Registration Authority. Clause 3(5) of CGO No.05 seeks to retain for the Customs Department “the right to call back the sold vehicle in case same is required to be presented before any judicial forum or court of law.” It therefore contemplates that such vehicles may constitute case property in sub-judice matters and their production may be required before a court of law to determine the status/title of such vehicles. Unlike Section 201 of the Customs Act, that requires goods to be sold in a public auction, clause 4 of CGO No.05 provides for an opaque mechanism for sale by requiring Customs authorities to regularly Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 108 inform/circulate the details of tampered vehicles ripe for disposal to eligible departments. Clause (iv)(ii) of CGO No.05 similarly does not create a mechanism for determining the fair value of disposable vehicles, but provides that the sale/token price of these vehicles shall be determined in accordance with its make, model and physical condition.

162. Despite repeated directions, the Customs authorities failed to provide any documentation to establish how disposal of vehicles and price determination was being undertaken in a transparent manner. When asked as to why such vehicles could not be disposed of through a regular auction, the response was that the vehicles could not be allowed to ply on the roads due to security concerns and also because such vehicles could not be registered by private individuals. It was the contention of the Customs Department that were tampered vehicles to be used by private individuals, their cloned identities would be a security concern. However, if such vehicles are in possession of Government departments, being used by officials of such departments, no security concerns arise. Likewise, when asked as to why the vehicles could not be sold through an auction process and registered by the successful bidders, when CGO No.05 required that such vehicles were to be registered with MRAs by the purchasing Departments, no satisfactory answer was furnished. When asked as to the quantum of revenue that was being lost by virtue of not putting the confiscated vehicles through an auction process for sale to the highest bidder, the Customs Department filed a report dated 10.05.2025.

163. The starting point of the Customs Department argument is that confiscated vehicles cannot be auctioned and can only be Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 109 sold as scrap. The value of all vehicles confiscated in the last five years when sold as scrap was projected by the Customs Department to be approximately Rs.250 million. The report however also provided that the replacement value of such vehicles i.e. if such vehicles were to be replaced with vehicles purchased by the Federal Government, would amount to approximately Rs.9,354 million.

164. There are various legal concerns that mar CGO No.05 and CGO dated 11.07.2007 issued under the garb of implementing ECC decision dated 03.03.2006. This Court has previously highlighted the limitations placed on the freedom of the Government to act at its whim in terms of Article 4 of the Constitution. It was held in Usama Khilji vs. Federation of Pakistan (Writ Petition No.1561 of 2023) that, “the government in a rule of law polity is a government of limited powers as it can only do what the law permits it to do. Article 4 of the Constitution, which articulates the right of individuals to be dealt with in accordance with law, summarizes this framework, whereby individuals are free to do what the law doesn't prohibit them from doing and the state can only do what the law authorizes it to do.”

165. The Federation and the Customs Authorities were repeatedly asked to assist the Court as to the relevant statutory provisions under which the ECC had issued directions for the disposal of vehicles confiscated under provisions of the Customs Act. No statutory provision was brought to the notice of the Court.

166. Section 219 of the Customs Act that vests in the FBR the power to make rules, includes, inter alia, the power to make Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 110 rules in relation to “any other matter necessary for giving effect to the provisions of this Act,” other than the matters listed in Third Schedule of the Customs Act. The CGOs, mentioned above, are admittedly not rules framed in terms of Section 219 of the Customs Act. The ECC is vested with no overriding power and authority under the Customs Act to determine the manner in which vehicles confiscated in terms of provisions of the Customs Act are to be disposed of.

167. As has been discussed above, the proviso to Section 182 of the Customs Act vests limited power in the FBR to authorize the use of confiscated vehicles (limited to use by officials of the FBR or its subordinate officers for operational purposes). The Customs Act vests no authority in the Federal Government or the FBR to undertake private sales of confiscated vehicles to Government and Semi-Government departments in an opaque manner that does not result in realizing the maximum value from the sale of state property for the benefit of the public exchequer.

168. It is evident from their content that CGO dated 11.07.2007 and CGO No.05 exceed the scope of power vested in the FBR in terms of Section 182 of the Customs Act. These instruments are ultra vires the parent Act pursuant to which they have been issued. The principles regulating the manner in which delegated legislation is to be promulgated and the authority to issue administrative instructions in discharge of delegated authority is to be exercised apply squarely to the question of legality of the CGOs in question. The CGOs go beyond the provisions of the Customs Act, including, inter alia, Section 182, and cannot be allowed to override or modify the parent law. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 111 169. It is settled that the State is not at liberty to dispense its largesse in an arbitrary manner and that arbitrary, discriminatory or non-transparent conferral of largesse violates public statutory duties, constitutional rights and principles of the equality guaranteed by the Constitution.

170. It was explained by the Supreme Court in Suo Motu Case No.13 of 2009 (PLD 2011 SC 619) that, “transparency lies at the heart of every transaction entered into by, or on behalf of, a public body. To ensure transparency and fairness in contracts, inviting of open bids is a prerequisite.” It was reiterated in Khwaja Muhammad Asif vs. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2014 SC 206) that, “any transaction which is not transparent and goes against the interests of the general public constitutes violation of Article 9 of the Constitution.”

171. The Supreme Court has endorsed the law laid down by the Indian Supreme Court in Ram and Shyam Company vs. State of Haryana and others (AIR 1985 SC 1147), wherein it was held that, “disposal of public property partakes the character of a trust in that in its disposal there should be nothing hanky panky and that it must be done at the best price so that larger revenue coming into the coffers of the State administration would serve public purpose… where disposal is for augmentation of revenue and nothing else, the State is under an obligation to secure the best market price available in a market economy.” In Ram and Shyam Company, the Indian Supreme Court endorsed a dissenting opinion rendered in Punnen Thomas vs. State of Kerala (AIR 1969 Kerala 81), which noted that, “the Government is not and should not be as free as an individual in selecting the recipients for largess. Whatever its Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 112 activity the Government is still the Government and will be subject to restraints, inherent in its position in a democratic society. A democratic Government cannot lay down arbitrary and capricious standards for the choice of persons with whom alone it will deal.”

172. The Customs Department in support of its contention that public auction of confiscated vehicles with tampered chassis numbers generate security concerns relied on judgments of the Lahore High Court in Khawar Shabbir vs. Members Judicial/Technical, Customs Excise and Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal (2008 PTD 1928) and Muhammad Sajjad vs. State (2014 PCr.LJ 1733). Perusal of the judgments reflects that they include scant reasoning to support the conclusion that vehicles with tampered chassis numbers must not be allowed to ply on roads as they constitute a security threat. That vehicles are cloned for use in criminal activities is well understood. But why are tampered vehicles only a threat when being used by private individuals and not when in the use of public officials?

173. There is no denying that a vehicle with a cloned identity cannot be allowed on the roads as in the absence of certainty that the particulars reflected in the registration documents of the vehicle relate to the vehicle in question, neither the safety of the vehicle as a driving machine nor the identity of the owner of the vehicle can be confirmed. This much is not contested by anyone. The question that arises is with regard to the fate of a vehicle that has been confiscated for having been found to be smuggled and therefore the product of an illegal activity, after the Customs Department has discharged the legal onus in such regard. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 113 174. This Court had issued notices to the MRA and the Excise and Taxation Officer appeared to assist the Court. It was submitted on the behalf of the MRA that creating a new VIN for a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is not problematic and can easily be done. Similarly, a separate number series can be issued for purposes of registration of vehicles with tampered chassis numbers to give them a verifiable identity, even in the event that their previous identity has been besmirched or cloned. The Court was informed that even presently the practice is that vehicles with tampered chassis numbers sold to Government departments are issued registration numbers to enable them to be driven around.

175. It is logically understandable that there is need for a verifiable vehicle identity. The chassis number of a vehicle referred to as the VIN is used for such purpose as a proxy. Where the chassis number has been tampered due to an accident or due to corrosion or deliberately for purposes of cloning the identity of the vehicle, the safety and identity of the vehicle no longer remains verifiable. But this can be fixed by creating unique VINs for tampered vehicles through a regulated process overseen by MRA and by creating a separate series of registration numbers for such vehicles, which would have the effect of such vehicles being sold at a discount, but would prevent them from becoming unusable and would also put on notice any subsequent buyers with regard to the tampering of the original chassis number. Such allocation of a VIN by State authorities would then take care of the concerns with regard to lack of identity and/or use of such vehicles in criminal activities Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 114 due to their owners being untraceable or having the benefit of plausible deniability.

176. The contrary approach being followed by the FBR pursuant to CGO No.05 is completely irrational, other than being illegal. A vehicle with a tampered chassis number and an unverifiable identity continues to generate security as well as vehicle safety concerns, irrespective of who is driving it around. The concern regarding a private individual driving a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is that the true identity of the vehicle is not verifiable. The concern remains equally applicable where such vehicle is being driven by a public official.

177. The report filed by the FBR, stating that the replacement value of confiscated vehicles being used by Government departments under provisions of CGO No.5 is significant, reflects that the use by public officials of private vehicles confiscated for being tempered is deliberate policy. From a policy perspective, this creates perverse incentives for the Customs Department and thus a conflict of interest when it comes to exercise of detention, seizure and confiscatory powers under provisions of the Customs Act. While Customs officials are fiduciaries, they have an incentive to exercise their police and adjudicatory powers to confiscate vehicles, which can then be employed for the benefit of officials within the Customs Department and other Government departments. The corresponding loss is that to the public exchequer. Instead of maximizing the value to be added to the public exchequer by sale of vehicles through a transparent auction process fetching the right market value, the confiscated vehicles are sold off to other Government departments in a nontransparent manner at a pittance. This undermines the principles Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 115 of transparency and equality in sale of state property, adversely affects the interests of Revenue, creates perverse incentives for law enforcement, and results in distribution of State largesse in a whimsical manner for the hand-picked public officials.

178. We need not get into individual cases in significant detail to document abuse of authority by the Customs Department in relation to use of confiscated vehicles. One example may suffice to illustrate the point. In Customs Reference No.12, this court ordered that the confiscated vehicle be handed to the owner. The order was not complied with. When the owner brought forth a contempt application, it turned out the vehicle, purportedly sold to the Archeology Department of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, was being used by a Commissioner of the Tax Department in Karachi. This was not acknowledged by the Customs Department, but established by a report filed by the Inspector General Police Sindh. When the vehicle was finally recovered, to be handed over to the owner, it came fitted with a fake number plate, which belonged to a Sukuzi Alto having been issued by the MRA in Sindh. The relevant Collector feigned ignorance re the use of such vehicle in Sindh (after initially suggesting the KP Archeology Department may have a branch office in Karachi), and placed the blame for installation of the fake number plate on minions within the department.

179. The record establishes that high value vehicles such as Land Cruisers etc. with a market value ranging from Rs 20-40 million are handed over to select officials across Government departments, with the relevant departments paying anything between Rs.50,000/- and Rs.100,000/- as cost of such vehicles. The invidious effects include lack of safe custody of case Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 116 property, due to an eagerness to employ such property for the use of public officials and its premature sale even while the matter remains sub-judice before adjudication authorities. This undermines the requirements of due process and fair adjudication. The ancillary effect of such perverse practice is delay and/or refusal by Customs authorities to abide by orders of adjudicatory authorities to release vehicles to their owners. In many instances where the Tribunal orders the release of a vehicle, the vehicle is seldom handed over to the owner on the basis that the remedy of filing a reference is being availed before the High Court in the absence of any stay order. In some cases where this Court passed explicit orders that the vehicle was to be retained in the Customs warehouse and not used during the pendency of the reference, it was brought to the attention of the Court that the the vehicle remained under continuing use of Customs officials in defiance of court orders. As a consequence of CGO No.5 (i) private property is converted to public use without payment of any compensation, even in cases where the Court ultimately comes to the conclusion that the vehicle is not smuggled and therefore not liable to confiscation, and (ii) possession of a vehicle by public officials and its continuing use during the pendency of the adjudicatory process undermines the state‘s case, rendering it impossible to determine the timing and liability for tampering of the chassis number.

180. There are two other deleterious consequences of the policy in place under the aforementioned CGOs. One, the policy of dealing with vehicles with tampered chassis numbers, instead of preventing the entry of smuggled vehicles with tampered chassis number into the country, has had the effect of facilitating Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 117 the entry and use of such vehicles. If a vehicle with a tampered chassis number is seized at a border post, it is not refused entry or dismantled and sold off as scrap. Instead, it is treated as a smuggled vehicle with a tampered chassis number and sold to a Government department for use in Pakistan. This facilitates the entry and use of smuggled vehicles into the country, while also permanently disabling the resale of such vehicles in terms of the CGOs in field. And two, such policy creates a disincentive to come up with a comprehensive policy framework to regulate the entire ecosystem that permits smuggling of vehicles into the country and/or the continuing use of smuggled vehicles with tampered chassis plates. The consequence being that the population of such smuggled vehicles with tampered chassis numbers continues to grow, defeating the objects of the Customs Act.

181. We are only concerned here with adjudication of questions of law and legality of acts of confiscation brought before us as a matter of law. It is not for this Court to make policy prescriptions or issue directions to curb various invidious practices incidentally referred to in this judgment. That would fall beyond the scope of our jurisdiction. However, as part of the adjudication of these references, our attention has been drawn by the learned counsels for the parties appearing before us to best international practices where other jurisdictions have employed logical and transparent mechanisms for purposes of branding and handling salvage, rebuilt salvage, junk and other calamity damaged vehicles. State authorities in such jurisdictions have come up with mechanisms to brand vehicles such that where the identity, value or safety of a vehicle is affected, an appropriate Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 118 brand/label is attached to such vehicle as part of the registration process to put buyers and/or prospective buyers on notice as to the status of such vehicle. Whether the chassis number of a vehicle is damaged or tampered due to an accident, corrosion, theft or any other act of trying to clone the vehicle, it is for State authorities as regulators and fiduciaries to brand the vehicle appropriately so that the antecedents of such vehicle, including tampered chassis number, is naturally brought to the attention of a diligent buyer. And where the vehicle is such that it can no longer be used on roads due to safety or security concerns, the vehicle is taken out of commission by virtue of the refusal of the MRA to register the same and/or cancel the registration previously granted, in consonance with a reasonable regulatory framework providing for such branding. The inscription of a State granted VIN as part of the regulatory framework to deal with tampered chassis number can easily be made part of such framework. The interpretation of Articles 9, 23 and 24 of the Constitution naturally requires that regulation, which is least restrictive for the enjoyment of property rights of vehicle owners, be given precedence over a sledgehammer approach that triggers confiscation over any other outcome, in disregard of the requirement of establishing fault on part of a property owner before subjecting him/her to a penalty of confiscation.

182. The best practices from other jurisdictions reflect that the entire cycle and ecosystem surrounding the import/purchase and use of vehicles is effectively regulated with vehicles being declared roadworthy on an annual basis subject to inspections. The verification of the VIN (including the cassis number) can easily be a part of such regulatory framework to ensure that Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 119 while the legitimate interests of the State in preventing smuggling and ensuring that imported vehicles are only released upon payment of taxes and duties is achieved, the police powers of the State are exercised in a manner that is least restrictive to the rights of citizens to liberty and property.

183. While clarifying the law with regard to the manner in which FSL reports are to be prepared in order to be reliable, High Courts have continued to issue directions that such reports must be prepared in the presence of the owner of the vehicle. Notwithstanding such directions, the practice of detaining, seizing and confiscating vehicles on the grounds that their chassis numbers are tampered, continues on the basis of FSL reports prepared without associating vehicle owners with the examination process. Similarly, the Supreme Court, while enumerating the law in relation to Section 156(1)(89) and (90) read with Section 2(s) of the Customs Act, directed in Abdul Karim, as a means to prevent the abuse of law and curb smuggling while giving effect to provisions of the Customs Act, that the Customs Department “should work out some collaborated efforts before and at the time of registration of such vehicles so that this menace may come to an end. A proper joint effort in registration may be a way out.” This direction can be complied with by ensuring that the Customs Department seeks the issuance of an FSL report to verify the particulars of all vehicles at the time of import. And likewise, the MRAs also seeks the issuance of an FLS report at the time of registration and rere-registration of each vehicle. This will enable the state to satisfy the evidentiary test laid down by the Supreme Court in Abdul Karim. Where all vehicles duly imported and released Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 120 after Customs‘ scrutiny and all vehicles duly registered and reregistered are supported by FSL reports, such documentation in support of legally imported and registered vehicles will make it easier for the state to establish genuine cases of smuggling.

184. The failure of Executive authorities to put together an effective regulatory and preventive framework such that smuggling of vehicles is prevented and deterred falls within the policy domain. As already noted, it is not for this Court to issue directions for adoption of a certain policy. The Executive authorities are free to choose between available policies options, so long as such policies operate within the framework of the law. However, there is no room for application of judicial restraint where Executive authorities adopt a policy framework that fall fouls of requirement of the law and the Constitution. It is in this context that this Court has scrutinized the regime put together by the Customs authorities, in purported compliance of ECC directives, manifested through the CGOs discussed above, which have been found to be ultra vires provisions of the Customs Act.

185. As has been explained above, the Customs authorities are not vested with power and jurisdiction to dispose of or put to use seized and/or confiscated vehicles till such time that a dispositive judgment with regard to the status of such vehicle has been passed by the Tribunal, or in case a reference is filed against the judgment of the Tribunal, by the High Court. The Executive is, however, at liberty to come up with a policy framework to dispose of or otherwise employ for its use vehicles that are confiscated and the title in relation to which vests in the Federal Government, so long as such policies are in accordance with law and any disposal of vehicles is in accordance with the principles Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 121 of transparency and equality laid down by the Supreme Court in the context of public officials dealing with State largesse.

186. Before we summarize and conclude our legal analysis, and highlight the principles of law applicable to the facts of the references being adjudicated, let us contextualize this discussion. The starting point of a conversation about constitutional rights is the manner in which rights and responsibilities are to be balanced in the context of the relationship between the citizen and the State. The laws put in place under the framework of the Constitution are conceived as a means of social control for the purpose of regulating individual behavior. It is in this context that the fault element in individual conduct becomes a prerequisite for purposes of imposition of a sanction on citizens.

187. The preventive aim of penal law cannot be served by crafting a standard of liability for imposing penalties that does not require a fault element: deterrence requires rational reflection by an individual and is linked to moral agency (manifested by individual autonomy and capacity) and consequent responsibility. An individual who does not know that he is indulging in wrongdoing or is committing an illegal or prohibited act, cannot be deterred from doing so by virtue of the punishment that may follow. It is thus that law assumes that the intent of the Legislature while crafting law cannot be to punish a person who lacks the capacity or ability to conform his behavior to the required standard prescribed by law. The demands of administrative efficiency certainly have a role to play in any penal system. But the State's need for such efficiency cannot be applied in a manner that upends the foundational objects of the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 122 penal system. The demand for efficiency cannot trump the fault element that must exist for imposition of punishment (except in limited cases involving strict liability offences that we are not dealing with here).

188. The cases before us involve application of clauses (9), (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act. The first thing to note about Section 156 of the Customs Act is that it deals with offences and penalties in a consolidated fashion such that the constituent elements of an offence on the basis of which an individual liable for such offence can be prosecuted and subjected to jail time are no different even for purposes of imposition of civil forfeitures. In other words, while the offence and/or penalty is defined in identical terms, whether the penalty is to be applied while following the criminal justice framework or while adopting the civil adjudicatory framework becomes relevant in terms of imposition of penalties. Thus, notwithstanding whether a penalty is a consequence of civil adjudication or criminal prosecution, the constituent elements of the offence are identical and must be established in the first instance. And where the constituent elements of an offence require the establishment of a fault element or mens rea, such fault is required to be established before the matter can move on to the stage of imposition of penalties. In this regard, the key difference between the civil adjudicatory framework and the criminal prosecution framework is that in the latter, it is for the State to establish its case beyond all reasonable doubt, while in the former, the legal onus of proof stands discharged if a case is established on the balance of probabilities. What is relevant for our purposes is that the fault element as part of the definition of Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 123 the offence remains the same in both cases. Clause (9) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act speaks of import or export of goods ―evading payment of leviable customs duties or in violation of any prohibition or restriction‖ on the import or export of the goods in question. The element of fault is built into the definition of the offence under the said clause. Likewise, clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act include within the definition of the offence elements such as a person acting ―without lawful excuse‖, and ―dealing with smuggling goods or any goods in respect to which there may be reasonable suspicion that they are smuggled goods‖ and goods in relation to which there is reasonable suspicion that any prohibition or restriction in law in relation to them has been contravened. In a nutshell, all the three offences that we are dealing with include a fault element within the description of the offence, which is required to be established before one can move on to the stage of imposing penalties.

189. It is in this backdrop that the penal system cannot turn a blind eye to the ecosystem within which smuggling takes place and tampered vehicles come into use within the country in terms of the matrix of rights and responsibilities between the State and the citizens. The definition of smuggling, as explained by the Supreme Court in Abdul Karim, focuses on vehicles brought into the country other than through a declared custom post or in relation to which evasion of payment of customs duties or taxes is established. Given the control now exercised by the State over its borders, there are not many opportunities for individuals to smuggle in goods as large as vehicles. The borders and custom posts on such borders fall within the control of the Executive Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 124 authorities of the State. To the extent that vehicles are released from such customs posts without payment of requisite duties and taxes, such customs posts fall within the control of and function under the scrutiny of Executive authorities. Once vehicles are released by Customs authorities, they are registered by MRAs that also fall under the control of Executive authorities. Vehicles brought into the country and not registered by MRAs are subject to the oversight and control by MRAs and police authorities, as the law prohibits vehicles from being driven around without being registered.

190. It is within this ecosystem of State control over various stages of the process through which a vehicle is brought into the country and then registered, that the question of the subsequent purchaser of a registered vehicle arises in circumstances where the Customs authorities assert that the chassis number of a vehicle is tampered. It is in this overall context that the question of protection of property rights of individual owners arises on the one hand, and the question of possession of a vehicle with a tampered chassis number arises on the other, with a presumption overhanging such a vehicle that it is smuggled. It is in this perspective that the question of interpretation of the constituent elements of offences defined under Section 156(1) of the Customs Act and the manner in which onus of proof is to be discharged by the individual owner and by the State in terms of Section 187 read with the relevant sub-clause of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act, is to be dealt with.

191. Let us now summarize the legal analysis and the relevant principles identified above that are applicable to cases where clauses (9), (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 125 are employed by Customs authority to seek confiscation of vehicles alleged to have tampered chassis numbers: i. The notion of an action in rem resulting in civil forfeiture/confiscation of property does not operate as a carve out against the right to own, possess and dispose of property guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution. Within our constitutional framework all that an action in rem signifies is that the penalty imposed in terms of Section 156(1) is limited to the action taken against the property and no assumptions with regard to the culpability of the owner of the property in question can be made on the basis of such action. The penal action is an outcome of adjudicatory proceedings and not criminal prosecution, the standard of proof is balance of probabilities and not beyond reasonable doubt, and the defence of double jeopardy is not available to the owner of the property in the event that the State chooses to prosecute him and adjudge whether or not he/she is liable as a criminal matter.

ii. Merely because there is no stigma attached to the person of the owner of the property being confiscated does not mean that civil forfeiture/confiscation of property is not a penalty. Such penalty is a consequence of the finding that the offence as defined in the relevant clause under Section 156(1) of the Customs Act is made out, and that the constituent elements of the offence as described in the relevant clause stand established, including, inter alia, the fault Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 126 element that is required to be established. Except in limited cases where the legislative intent as manifest from the words used to define and characterize an offence clearly establishes that the offence is designed as a strict liability offence, the presumption remains that the Legislature seeks to impose a penalty following the finding of culpability, notwithstanding whether the penalty is a consequence of civil adjudication or criminal prosecution.

iii. The guarantee of due and fair process provided by Article 10A of the Constitution applies equally whether proceedings involve determination of civil liabilities or criminal charges. The principles of natural justice as well as the principle of causation in finding fault and the principle of proportionality when it comes to imposition of penalty is a subset of the right to procedural and substantive constitutional due process guaranteed by Article 10A read with Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution, when the punishment involves dispossession of property. The doctrine of reasonability and proportionality as employed by Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution require that any enforcement action taken for purposes of upholding the law should constitute the least restrictive means to realize a legitimate state objective where it impinges on protected property rights.

iv. Chapter XVII of the Customs Act vests broad police powers in officials of the Customs Department for purposes of prevention of smuggling. Such powers must be exercised in a manner that is least restrictive Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 127 to the enjoyment of the rights of owners of vehicles, when it comes to exercise of such powers in departmental action that has the effect of denying a vehicle owner the right to continue to possess and enjoy his/her property. This entails, inter alia, that a vehicle cannot be detained and/or seized on suspicion alone. Where there exists prima facie basis to detain and seize a vehicle, such seizure can be ordered while letting the vehicle remain within the possession of the owner in terms of the guidance provided in the later part of section 168(1) of the Customs Act, except where seizure is deemed essential for safe custody of case property in a case where there is reasonable basis for the Customs Department to suspect that the property will be made to disappear.

v. Any seized vehicle that constitutes case property must be detained in safe custody in a manner that is verifiable, and the state can establish before adjudicatory authorities that the detained vehicle was not left unmonitored such that tampering of its chassis number could possibly transpire after such seizure. Where the tampering of the chassis number is the primary basis for an allegation that the vehicle is smuggled and its identity has been cloned, it is for the Customs Department having seized the vehicle and taken it into custody, to establish through credible material that such tampering took place prior to the seizure of the vehicle and not thereafter.

vi. Where the FSL report is the primary basis to establish that the chassis number is tampered, such FSL report Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 128 must be the product of a process where the Customs Department is able to establish that the vehicle was safely transmitted for forensic examination, while associating the owner of the vehicle with such process. The FSL report must follow prescribed protocols in accordance with best international practices, keeping in view the safety features used by vehicle manufacturers, to give a definitive report that the vehicle identity is besmirched and none of the VIN numbers inscribed on the vehicle can be traced and matched to the particulars reflected on the registration and import documents related to the vehicle.

vii. The tampering of the chassis plate is not definitive proof of the act of smuggling, which needs to be established on a balance of probabilities and an FSL report is part of the evidence/material for purposes of discharging such legal onus. However, where the vehicle is not retained in safe custody by the Customs Department after seizure and the FSL report is not the outcome of examination of a safely transmitted vehicle, such report is of limited evidentiary value for purposes of discharge of legal onus by the Customs Department that the vehicle is smuggled.

viii. The initial onus of proof in terms of section 187 read with clauses (89) and (90) of section 156(1) of the Customs Act is on the owner of the vehicle to make out a prima facie case establishing a lawful excuse to possess the vehicle. The registration document establishing title of the vehicle owner is sufficient for purposes of establishing such prima facie case. In Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 129 relation to a vehicle the import/auction/registration of which was is five years old, the Customs Department lacks legal basis to demand import documents from the registered owner of the vehicle in view of section 211 of the Customs Act. In cases where the limitation period in terms of section 211 of the Customs Act has not expired, the evidentiary burden to establish a prima facie case remains with the vehicle owner. But the ultimate legal burden to establish that the vehicle is smuggled rests with the Customs Department.

ix. The exception in relation to lack of lawful excuse for possessing a vehicle with a tampered chassis plate, as explained in Abdul Karim, applies only “where it is established [by the Customs Department] that the chassis/engine numbers have been tampered with after auction or registration to match the description of the auctioned or registered vehicle.” The expansive policing and investigation powers provided under Chapter 3 of the Customs Act are to be employed by the Customs Department to gather relevant material/evidence to establish on a balance of probabilities that the vehicle with the tempered chassis plate is in fact a smuggled vehicle. Such investigation would require, for example, that the Customs Department investigate a case where the allegation is that the seized vehicle with tampered chassis number has been cloned to project the identity of another vehicle duly imported and registered, and determine the whereabouts of the lawfully imported/registered vehicle to establish on a balance Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 130 of probabilities that seized vehicle is in fact a smuggled and cloned vehicle.

x. The owner of a vehicle with a tampered chassis number would have a lawful excuse to own/possess such vehicle, even if it is determined as a matter of fact that the chassis plate of the vehicle is tampered, if he/she succeeds in establishing that such owner is a bona fide purchaser, having paid full market value for the vehicle, and with no notice or suspicion that the vehicle in question was smuggled and/or that taxes/duties in relation to such vehicle were not paid by the original importer/owner. Payment for full market value through verifiable banking channels would establish that the vehicle was not purchased at a discount, as a discounted value could logically raise suspicion with a prudent purchaser re the credentials of the vehicle. The defence of being a bona fide purchaser for full value without notice is available in adjudicatory proceedings under the Customs Act, as there is no provision within the Customs Act read with Articles 9, 10A, 23 and 24 of the Constitution that would deny the owner of a property, who is not found to be at fault or culpable, to be unable to raise such defence for protection of his/her property rights. xi. The confiscation of a vehicle through proceedings in rem can only take place (resulting in vesting of the title of property owned by a private individual in the Federal Government) after it is established, on a balance of probabilities, that the vehicle was smuggled and the owner of such vehicle is liable to be divested Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 131 of his title, as such owner has failed to discharge his/her onus to establish a lawful excuse to own/possess such vehicle. The divestment of private title and vesting of title in the government does not operate in the same manner as the concept of superior title operates in the case of theft where another individual is found to have a superior title to the stolen property, that predates the title of a subsequent bona fide purchaser. In case of civil forfeiture in relation to the offence of smuggling, a private individual can only be divested of his title to private property once it is established by the State in accordance with law that the property is the product of an illegal activity, and the owner/possessor of such property is culpable, either due to acts of commission or due to his/ her failure to establish lawful excuse to be in possession of such property. The state has no prior superior title to such property and the state's title to such property is a consequence of establishment of the fact that the property is the product of an illegal act i.e. smuggling.

xii. Till such time that the private individual is divested of his/her title to property and the vehicle in question vests in the Federal Government after establishment of the fact that the vehicle is smuggled by virtue of a dispositive judgment by adjudicatory authorities established under provisions of the Customs Act, which finding has attained finality, the Customs Department is vested with no authority to dispose of the vehicle, which constitutes case property, or put Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 132 such case property to use, while the matter is subjudice, in breach of the requirements of safe custody and safe disposal of property, as well as the principles of separation of powers that require judicial oversight over executive actions when it comes to determination of civil rights and liabilities in terms of Article 10A read with Article 175 of the Constitution.

xiii. Once the vehicle stands forfeited in terms of section 182 of the Customs Act, it can be disposed of or employed by the state for its use in accordance with law and the principles of transparency attracted to the disposal and/or use of public property, that do not allow the state to dispense largesse in an arbitrary manner or in a manner where public functionaries dealing with public property suffer from conflict of interest.

xiv. The State owes a duty of care to citizens and is under an obligation to put in place the requisite policy framework to prevent and deter smuggling, which is one of the primary objects of the Customs Act. Such policy framework must be in consonance with the State‘s obligation to create legal certainty with regard to the rights and obligations of citizens in order to guide their conduct. As held in Abdul Karim, the State is under an obligation to ensure that the Customs Department and the MRAs, as arms of the State, coordinate mechanisms and exercise diligence. This can be done by requiring FSL reports at the time of Customs clearance of vehicles and registration/reregistration of vehicles to ensure that the presumption Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 133 of correctness that attaches to actions of state officials holds, and administrative malfeasance does not result in enabling smuggling and/or registration of smuggled vehicles. The State cannot employ provisions of the Customs Act as a weapon to trap innocent owners of property, and commandeer or forfeit such assets for its own use without payment of compensation. The sanction of forfeiture of a vehicle on the basis that it is smuggled must always follow the establishment of fault element on part of the owner whose property is to be confiscated.

192. Let us now revert to where we started and answer the questions of law that arise in these references and were articulated in paragraphs 2 and 3 of this judgment. Is an FSL report finding tampering dispositive of smuggling?

193. No. Tampering triggers a rebuttable presumption under Section 187A. The initial burden to establish ―lawful excuse‖ or ―lawful justification‖ to own/possess the vehicle rests with the vehicle owner. Once the vehicle owner makes out a prima facie case to establish him/herself as the bonafide owner of the vehicle, the particulars of which are listed in the certificate of registration issued by the MRA, the onus of proof shifts to the State. The State must then rebut the presumption and discharge the legal burden to establish ―smuggling‖ as defined in Section 2(s) on a balance of probabilities.
Can a vehicle with a tampered chassis be released, or must it always be confiscated?

194. It can be released to the owner if they establish a ―lawful excuse,‖ such as being a bona fide purchaser for full value Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 134 without notice of illegality. Confiscation in favor of the State is only permissible upon the State establishing a fault element on the part of the owner, as required in terms of the offense as defined in the relevant clause of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act.
Can a penalty be imposed without a finding of wrongdoing against the owner?

195. No. A penalty under clauses (9), (89), and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act cannot be imposed without a finding of culpability or negligence on the part of the owner. It is ―harsh‖ (as stated in Abdul Karim) and thus ―grossly unjust‖ to confiscate the property of a wholly innocent person used without their consent or knowledge. The State must establish a fault element before a penal sanction can be lawfully applied. Is the penalty imposed in rem on the property or in personam on the owner?

196. While the procedural form of civil forfeiture is an action in rem against the property, it functions as a penalty that adversely affects the owner's constitutionally guaranteed property rights. Therefore, for such penalty to pass constitutional muster, it must be preceded by an in personam finding of liability or wrongdoing against the owner. The fiction of the ―guilty property‖ does not allow the State to bypass the requirement of establishing the owner's culpability before depriving him of his property rights by confiscating the same in favor of the State.
How are property rights and due process balanced against the State's interest in deterring smuggling?

197. The balance is achieved through the application of a three-pronged test and the principle of proportionality: Legality – the measure must be expressly provided for by law; Necessity – the measure must be directed toward a legitimate State Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 135 objective and be necessary to achieve the object of the statute that imposes the restriction; Proportionality – the measure must be the least restrictive means to realize the State‘s objective. The State cannot trap innocent owners to deter smugglers. Instead, it must use regulatory frameworks that protect bona fide purchasers while targeting the actual perpetrators. Does a confiscatory order qualify as the “least restrictive means” to realize a legitimate State objective?

198. Not necessarily. If a legitimate State objective (such as preventing the use of vehicles with unverified identities) can be achieved through less restrictive means—such as re-branding the vehicle with a new State-issued VIN or registering it under a unique series—then a blanket confiscation order fails the test of proportionality. Confiscation is only the ―least restrictive means‖ when the State can prove the owner is not a bona fide purchaser and lacks a ―lawful excuse‖ for possession of the vehicle with tampered particulars.
199. We can now apply the law as summarized above to the facts of the references before us.

Customs Reference No. 12/2022 200. This Court by short order dated 30.09.2025 allowed the reference and directed that the vehicle be released to the applicant forthwith. The vehicle was, however, not released. It had purportedly been sold to the Directorate of Archaeology and Museum, Peshawar, for Rs 100,000, but was being used by an Income Tax Commissioner in Sindh. In response to the civil miscellaneous application filed by the applicant, the Court issued notices to the relevant parties. It emerged in the proceedings that followed that the question of interpretation of Section 187A Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 136 of the Customs Act, introduced to the Finance Act, 2025, may be relevant for such proceedings. The matter was therefore listed for hearing along with other pending references that involved the question of confiscation of vehicles in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act for reasons recorded in order dated 22.10.2025.

201. On merits, this Court finds that the order of the Tribunal is not sustainable in the eyes of law for disregarding the principles of law that have been highlighted in this judgment. In terms of background, the vehicle in question was deemed to be smuggled, it was seized and was then ordered to be released pursuant to Order-in-Original No.7903/2013 upon payment of leviable duty and taxes along with redemption fine in terms of SRO 172(I)/2013 dated 05.03.2013. This order also noted that the vehicle would be liable to confiscation in the event that it was subsequently found to have a tampered chassis number.

202. Upon payment of duty in the amount of Rs.4,627,661, deposited with the Customs Department, the vehicle was regularized and the Customs Department issued a No Objection Certificate for registration of the vehicle on 07-05-2013. An order of the Customs Department regularizing a vehicle which is found to be smuggled, which notes that the release order would stand annulled if it is subsequently determined that the vehicle had a tempered chassis number, suffers from nonfeasance. Where the Customs Department, as an arm of the State, disposes off a vehicle upon payment of taxes and duties and or auctions it, such official act comes with a representation that the vehicle has a clean marketable title and the person purchasing such vehicle in auction proceedings, or otherwise assuming ownership of the vehicle on payment of taxes, duties and Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 137 redemption fine cannot be subsequently burdened with a liability merely because the Customs Department did not ensure at the relevant time that the chassis number was authentic and not tampered.

203. The vehicle was registered on 21.05.2014, with the MRA having satisfied itself that the Customs Department had issued an NOC for such purpose. The vehicle was then intercepted on 08.12.2020 by the Directorate General Intelligence and Investigation on suspicion of it being a smuggled vehicle, notwithstanding that it was duly registered with the MRA. The demand to produce import/amnesty documents on 08.12.2020 for a vehicle that was released by the Customs Department on 30.03.2013 and registered on 21.05.2014, fell afoul the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Abdul Kareem. This the Tribunal did not take into account. It further did not take into account the infirmities from the date of its detention and seizure, including, inter alia, that the vehicle was not kept in safe custody and remained in use of public officials. According to the record, the vehicle was purportedly referred for examination to the FSL on 23.11.2020, which was prior to the date of its interception i.e. 08.12.2020. The owner of the vehicle was never associated with the examination of the vehicle. Once the applicant was able to establish himself as a bona fide owner of the vehicle by providing the relevant registration record as well as details of the regularization of the vehicle and payment of taxes and duties pursuant to Customs Department's Order-in-Original No.7903/2013, the onus of proof shifted to the Customs Department to establish that the vehicle in question was not that that was regularized through the aforementioned order in an Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 138 amnesty scheme in 2013. Customs Department failed to discharge such onus and produce evidence to establish that the vehicle was smuggled or was not the one in relation to which taxes, duties and redemption fine had been paid in the year 2013.

204. It was for these reasons that the Court found that the vehicle was not liable to be confiscated and the applicant, as a bona fide owner, had discharged his onus of establishing that he was the subsequent purchaser of a vehicle that had been regularized by the Customs Department in an amnesty scheme in the year 2013. Being the owner of a duly registered vehicle, purchased for value without notice of any infirmity with regard to the title of the vehicle, his vehicle was not liable to be confiscated.

Custom Reference No. 77/2023 205. During the proceedings of this matter, the Court had invited experts from various forensic science laboratories, the Customs Department and the MRAs, to understand the phenomenon of tempering of chassis numbers. As part of the proceedings, the FBR also provided assistance, including by filing the relevant CGOs pursuant to which confiscated vehicles continue to be sold and used by public officials, as well as a report dated 10.05.2025, providing details of the number and value of confiscated vehicles being used by public officials. These matters have already been dealt with earlier in this judgment.

206. On merits, this Court notes that the vehicle was detained on 12.07.2021, its seizure was ordered on 09-08-2021 and a show-cause notice was issued to the applicant on 26-08-2021, with the Order-in-Original confiscating the vehicle being passed Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 139 on 19.10.2021. We have noted that there was a significant gap between the time of detention of the vehicle and its confiscation. There is nothing on record to establish that the vehicle was kept in safe custody in a manner that tampering of the chassis number after its detention could be ruled out. While setting aside the order of confiscation, the Tribunal took into account the fact that the Order-in-Original was issued beyond a period of thirty days from the issuance of the Show Cause Notice and was barred by limitation in terms of Section 179(3) of the Customs Act. And consequently, no penal action could flow from such Order-in- Original. The Tribunal noted that a second forensic examination was ordered by the Collector of Customs, but was not undertaken. The owner of the vehicle produced the relevant import documents, which had been verified by the Customs Appraisement Department (East), Karachi, by letter dated 29.07.2022. The owner thus established through the production of vehicle registration and import documents that he was a bona fide owner. The Customs Department, on the other hand, failed to produce any proof of smuggling and did not establish through record that the vehicle in question was not the vehicle, the particulars of which were mentioned in the import documents and registration documents. Given that the basic order of the Tribunal rests on the findings that the Order-in-Original was barred by limitation, the said finding is sufficient to dismiss the reference while upholding the order of the Tribunal. To the extent that the vehicle is still in the custody of the Customs Department, it will be handed over to the owner forthwith. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 140 Custom Reference No. 100/2023.

207. The vehicle in question was cleared under an amnesty scheme pursuant to SRO 172(I)/2013 dated 15.03.2013, and the vehicle owner provided proof that duties and taxes in the amount of Rs.2,163,424 had been deposited with the Customs Department on 29.03.2013. The vehicle, a 2007 Model Toyota Parado, was registered in Quetta. It was seized on 24.6.2020 on the basis that the chassis number was cut and welded. The Order-in-Original dated 29.07.2020, directed that the vehicle be released to the owner on the basis that the Customs Department had failed to establish that the vehicle in question was not the one that was cleared under the amnesty scheme 2013. The Tribunal set aside such order and directed that the vehicle be confiscated on the basis that the cut and welded chassis plate created doubt regarding the genuineness of the vehicle, and that the vehicles cleared in the amnesty scheme did not protect vehicles with cut and welded chassis numbers. The vehicle owner filed a petition before the Islamabad High Court to seek the release of the vehicle pending adjudication of the matter. Writ petition No. 2817 of 2020 was allowed by judgment dated 17.11.2020, directing the Customs Department to grant temporary custody to the vehicle owner. The Customs Department challenged this judgment before the Supreme Court, which refused leave by order dated 28.09.2020. Notwithstanding these judicial orders, the Customs Department refused to hand over possession of the vehicle to the vehicle owner. We have already noted earlier in this judgment that the State cannot seek to auction or regularize vehicles in an amnesty scheme while accepting duties and taxes and payment of consideration on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 141 one hand, and make such transaction conditional on a determination to be made at a subsequent time as to whether or not the chassis number of the vehicle is tampered. When a vehicle is cleared in an amnesty scheme or sold by the State in an auction, implicit in such process is the representation by the State that the vehicle comes with a clean and marketable title. This fundamental principle of fairness and state responsibility was not taken into account by the Tribunal. By virtue of producing the relevant amnesty documents along with record payment of duties and taxes and registration documents establishing that the applicant was bona fide owner of the vehicle, the applicant discharged prima facie onus of proof in terms of section 156(1) read with section 187 of the Customs Act. The onus then shifted to the Customs Department, which was required to establish through record that the vehicle in question was not the vehicle that was released under the amnesty scheme as claimed by the applicant and was in fact smuggled a vehicle, in terms of section 2(s) of the Customs Act. This the Customs Department failed to do as had been correctly held by the Collector in Order-in-Original dated 29.07.2020. We, therefore, find that the Tribunal erred in holding that the vehicle was liable to be confiscated without the Customs Department discharging its legal onus to establish that the vehicle was smuggled. The order is thus not sustainable in the eyes of law and is set aside. The Order-in-Original dated 27.09.2020, is upheld and the Customs Department is directed to hand over possession of the vehicle to the applicant forthwith to the extent that the vehicle is still in possession of the Customs Department. Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 142 Customs Reference No. 214/2023 208. The vehicle in question was ordered to be confiscated by Order-in-Original dated 24.11.2020. The Tribunal set aside such order on the basis that the forensic examination was undertaken and the FSL report produced without associating the owner of the vehicle. It further noted that the vehicle was lawfully registered and that the Customs Department had failed to produce any evidence of smuggling in relation to such vehicle.

209. We have taken note of the Order-in-Original, which reflects the contentions of the vehicle owner, who asserted that he purchased the vehicle from Raja Riaz Hussain on 05.12.2017 for an amount of Rs.900,000. The seller then disappeared and the vehicle owner filed an FIR 297/19 dated 03.04.2019, after having found that the vehicle had a tempered chassis number. As the last possessor of the vehicle, he was granted superdari of such vehicle after the original seller was declared a proclaimed offender. We find that the impugned order passed by the Tribunal is not sustainable in the eyes of law. The Tribunal did not take into account the fact that the question of tampering of the chassis number of the vehicle was not contested by the vehicle owner. On the contrary, it was the vehicle owner that had sought registration of an FIR against the individual who sold the vehicle to him on the basis that the vehicle was found to be tampered. In this factual background, the non-association of the vehicle owner while producing an FSL report was of no consequence, as the FSL report merely established the fact of tampering of the chassis number, which was not contested by the owner. It was then for the vehicle owner to establish that he was a bona fide purchaser of the vehicle for full value without Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 143 notice of any infirmity in the title of the vehicle. We are not convinced, on the basis of record, that the vehicle owner established the same. It is the vehicle owner's assertion that the vehicle was purchased for a price of Rs.900,000, which does not appear to be the full market value of such vehicle. The record further establishes that while the vehicle was purchased from Raja Riaz Hussain in 2017, its FSL was ordered by the vehicle owner himself in 2019. There is no explanation for what inspired the vehicle owner to solicit an FSL report two years after the purchase of the vehicle. The Tribunal ought to have determined, on the basis of record, whether the vehicle owner established as a prima facie matter that he was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice and had no basis to reasonably suspect that the vehicle may be tampered. This the Tribunal did not do. We, therefore, set aside the impugned order and remand the matter back to the Tribunal to consider the principles of law enumerated in this judgment and apply them to the facts of the case after affording the vehicle owner and the Customs Department an opportunity to be heard.

Custom Reference No. 05/2024 210. The applicant has been unable to convince us that the impugned order of the Tribunal upholding the Order-in-Original that the vehicle is liable to be confiscated suffers from legal infirmity and is liable to be set aside. The Order-in-Original was passed on the basis that the FSL report dated 17.08.2023 established that the chassis number of the vehicle was manually punched and the vehicle had been registered by using the import documents of another vehicle. The applicant contested that the FSL report had been produced without associating the vehicle owner. The Tribunal ordered a second examination on the Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 144 request of the applicant, while associating the applicant with the process. This report dated 08.12.2023, confirmed that the original chassis number had been erased and could not be deciphered due to deep grinding.

211. During the proceedings before this Court, the Customs Department established through record that the import documents being relied on by the owner of the seized vehicle related to a black Toyota Land Cruiser Model 2017. The engine and chassis number, as reflected in the import documents, matched the particulars of a vehicle registered in the province of Sindh, with registration number BT-0999, and was presently owned by Pir Syed Saleh Shah Jilani. The whereabouts of this vehicle had been tracked, which was present in Karachi, and pictorial evidence confirming its chassis number was collected. The import documents of such vehicle, as verified by the MRA, were the same documents that had been used to register the seized vehicle in the province of Punjab, which was given registration number AAH-49. In view of the record produced by the Customs Department, which established that the import documents being claimed by the owner of the seized vehicle related to another vehicle duly imported and registered in the province of Sindh, the Customs Department successfully established that the import documents being claimed by the applicant belonged to another vehicle. We had undertaken this exercise and allowed the Customs Department to produce relevant record of the duly imported and registered vehicle, to satisfy ourselves that the factual determination rendered by the Tribunal while upholding the confiscation of the vehicle was not perverse. Having satisfied ourselves thus, we find no reason to Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 145 interfere with the order of the Tribunal. The reference is decided in favor of the Customs Department.
Custom Reference No. 31/2024.

212. We have no reason to disagree with the order of the Tribunal, which set aside the Order-in-Original directing that the vehicle be confiscated. On merits, the Tribunal took into account the contention of the owner (who had produced import documents and proof of payment of customs duties, and the registration documents of the vehicle) that the vehicle was stolen, which was reported in FIR No.363/2019 dated 17.08.2019. It was recovered from Peshawar and custody was granted to the vehicle owner. The Tribunal took note of the fact that there was no rival claimant of the vehicle. The order of confiscation relied on a replaceable VIN plate located on the door jamb and a tampered chassis plate. The Tribunal noted that the vehicle owner was never confronted with the matter of the VIN number on the door jamb, and that confiscation was ordered on a basis beyond that stated in the show cause notice. The Tribunal concluded, as a matter of fact, that in terms of its physical attributes the vehicle was a 2015 model, and not a 2014 model, as asserted in the Order-in-Original. It also held that the FSL report did not automatically establish the fact of smuggling. The vehicle owner had discharged, prima facie, onus of proof by producing registration documents along with import and auction documents for the vehicle, while the Customs Department had failed to discharge its onus to establish that the vehicle was smuggled in terms of Section 2(s) of the Customs Act. The Tribunal also held that the Order-in-Original was passed after 50 days of issuance of the show cause notice and was therefore Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 146 barred by limitation, in terms of Section 179.3 of the Customs Act. And as held by the Supreme Court in Collector of Sales Tax, Gujranwala vs. Super Asia Mohammad Din and Sons (2017 SCMR 1427), no penal consequences could flow from such order. We accordingly find no reason to interfere with such order and direct that the custody of the vehicle be handed over to the applicant forthwith to the extent that it is still in possession of the Customs Department.

Custom Reference No.42/2024 213. The Customs Department has impugned the order of the Tribunal, which set-aside the Order-in-Original dated 10.11.2023, pursuant to which the vehicle was confiscated. The Tribunal took into account the fact that the show cause notice merely stated that the vehicle owner had failed to produce import/auction or amnesty documents, and the record of the vehicle was not found in PRAL database. The charge that the chassis number was tampered was not put to the applicant, but the confiscation of the vehicle was ordered on the basis that the chassis plate had been cut and welded. The Tribunal, on merits, concluded that the vehicle was the subject of a major accident. The accident was also reported in a police report. The vehicle owner also produced import documents reflecting the chassis number of the vehicle. The Tribunal did not agree with the conclusion drawn by the Customs Department that as the alteration in the chassis number plate had not been reported to the MRA in terms of Section 33 of the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, the owner‘s explanation that the vehicle was damaged in an accident was liable to be rejected. We have already held that the consequence of noncompliance with Section 33 of the Motor Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 147 Vehicles Ordinance is prescribed within the said law and can lead to suspension or cancellation of the vehicle‘s registration, if the facts and circumstances so warrant. But non-reporting of any alteration made to a vehicle cannot be made the basis to disregard a case made out by a vehicle owner, wherein the overall facts and circumstances of the case the owner succeeds in establishing that he/she is a bonafide owner of the vehicle, but the Customs Department fails to discharge its onus to establish that the vehicle was smuggled and/or the vehicle owner was liable for wrongdoing. In the instant case, the Customs Department brought on record no material or evidence establishing that the vehicle was smuggled, or that the vehicle had sought to clone the identity of another vehicle, the import documents of which had been used to register the vehicle in question. The Customs Department undertook no investigation to determine whether the vehicle suffered an accident, what was the nature of the accident, and whether any cutting and welding of the chassis plate could be a natural consequence of the bodywork required post-accident. We therefore find no reason to disagree with the factual determinations made by the Tribunal in holding that the respondent had established himself as a bona fide vehicle owner, but the Customs Department had failed to discharge its onus to establish the fact of smuggling. The Customs Department is directed to hand over custody of the vehicle to the applicant forthwith, to the extent that it is still in possession of the Customs Department.

Custom Reference No.61/2024 214. We are not convinced that the impugned order passed by the Tribunal suffers from legal infirmities and requires our Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 148 interference. The vehicle in question, a 2003 model Toyota Prado, was registered after verification of import documents by the Customs authorities and physical inspection of the vehicle as evident from the MRA report dated 02.02.2024. The vehicle was seized on the basis that the driver had failed to produce import documents, and that while the vehicle‘s import data was available in the PRAL database, the chassis number looked suspicious. In response to the Show-Cause Notice, the owner produced the relevant documents establishing the import of the vehicle from Japan and its registration in the year 2013, after the import documents having been verified by the Collectorate of Appraisement, Customs House, Karachi by letter dated 03.10.2013. On the basis of an FSL report that the chassis number was grinded and tampered, the Customs Department came to the conclusion that the import documents of some other legally imported vehicle had been used for registration of the vehicle in question. The Tribunal rendered a split decision. The Member judicial concluded that the owner was an innocent subsequent purchaser, who had paid full value for the vehicle, and had had the vehicle registered in his name after completion of all legal formalities, thus establishing himself as a bona fide owner. The Customs Authorities, on the other hand, had produced no record to establish that the chassis number in question, as reflected in the import documents, belonged to another vehicle. And no other imported vehicle with the said particulars was traced to establish that the seized vehicle was illegally cloned and therefore smuggled. The Member Technical disagreed with the opinion of Member Judicial. The referee Member agreed with Member Judicial and held that the owner had produced import documents as well as registration Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 149 documents, after which the onus of proof shifted to the Customs Department, which failed to discharge the same by establishing the allegation of smuggling.

215. The Tribunal held that the concept of a bona fide purchaser was not alien to the provisions of the Customs Act and even in view of the FSL report and the chassis numbers that were deciphered, it could not be definitively held that the original chassis number had been tampered due to the resemblance of the numbers as deciphered with the original chassis number. We find no reason to disagree with the factual determinations of the Tribunal and the manner in which principles of law were applied to the case at hand. We, therefore, direct that the custody of the vehicle be handed over to the applicant forthwith, to the extent that it is still in possession of the Customs Department. Custom Reference No.74/2024 216.
