We find that the order of the Tribunal upholding the Orderin-Original dated 02.01.2024, pursuant to which the vehicle in question was confiscated, is not sustainable in the eyes of law. The vehicle, a 2007 model Toyota Axio, was registered for the first time in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on 20.11.2007. It was seized on 28.09.2023. At such time, the Customs Department was vested with no authority to demand that the vehicle owner produces import documents in relation to the vehicle in view of the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Abdul Karim given that five-year limitation period prescribed under Section 211 of the Customs Act had longer expired. The Tribunal also did not take into account that the Order-in-Original was devoid of reasoning and articulated no basis for how the vehicle was found to be smuggled and liable for confiscation. The Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 150 Tribunal wrongly held that the concept of a bona fide purchaser was not applicable under provisions of the Customs Act, which aspect has been explained in detail in this judgment. By producing the registration documents, the vehicle owner has discharged the prima facie onus to establish that he was a bona fide owner of the vehicle. On the query of the Customs Department, the Excise and Taxation Department in Jaffarabad Sindh had refused to verify the import documents on the basis that the record of the office was burnt during riots after the assassination of Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto. Merely on the basis that over 17 years old import record maintained by a government department could not be verified by it, for no fault of the vehicle owner, the Tribunal came to the flawed conclusion that the vehicle owner had failed to discharge his onus under Section 187 of the Customs Act. As explained in detail in this judgment, by production of the relevant registration documents, the vehicle owner discharged his onus of proof as a prima facie matter. It was the Customs Department that was then required to rebut the presumption of correctness that attached to the registration documents, by establishing through record that the vehicle was indeed smuggled and that the vehicle owner was liable for wrongdoing. The Customs Department failed in discharging its legal onus and the vehicle is therefore not liable to be confiscated.

217. During the hearing, we were informed by the Customs Department that during the pendency of the matter, while it was subjudice before the Tribunal, the vehicle was auctioned. We were given no satisfactory explanation for why the vehicle was required to be auctioned in exercise of discretionary authority Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 151 under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act. As a matter of law, we have held in this judgment that a seized or confiscated vehicle cannot be disposed of till such time that the order of confiscation attains finality with the matter having been decided through dispositive judgments by the relevant adjudicatory authorities established under provisions of the Customs Act. We, therefore, direct that the entire auction amount received by the Customs Department in the auction proceedings, without any deductions, be handed over to the applicant forthwith and in no event beyond a period of 14 days. We further find that the manner in which authority has been exercised in this case under Section 169(4) of the Customs Act was arbitrary and not a fair, just and reasonable exercise of public authority. To the extent that such pre-mature auction has inflicted any financial loss on the applicant, he would be within his right to initiate appropriate civil proceedings for recovery of damages from the State, if so minded.

Customs Reference No. 07/2025 218. We find no reason to interfere with the order of the Tribunal that set aside the Order-in-Original dated 29.03.2024, pursuant to which the vehicle was ordered to be confiscated. The vehicle, a 2015 model Toyota Aqua, was purchased through an amnesty scheme auction. The vehicle owner produced the relevant auction documents along with registration documents to discharge prima facie proof of ownership. He also produced record of FIR No. 331/2018 dated 27.07.2018, whereby he had reported that the vehicle had been stolen. The vehicle was subsequently recovered and custody was handed over to the vehicle owner by judicial order dated 20.11.2018.

Notwithstanding the fact that the chassis number was found Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 152 tampered, the Additional Sessions Judge granting custody satisfied himself that the owner had the original car key and had been able to identify the vehicle by its peculiar features, including dents etc. The Tribunal found that the vehicle owner had discharged his onus of proof and that it could not be ruled out that the chassis number had been tampered by the car lifter, especially as the owner had established his prior possession and there was no other claimant of the vehicle. It further held that the Customs Department had failed to discharge the onus of establishing that the vehicle in question was not the vehicle the particulars of which had been provided by the vehicle owner, and established through record that the vehicle was smuggled. We find no infirmity with the manner in which the law has been applied to the facts of the case and find that the Tribunal correctly concluded that the vehicle was not liable to be confiscated. We therefore direct that the custody of the vehicle be handed over to the applicant forthwith, to the extent that it is still in possession of the Customs Department.

A. Rahman Abbasi Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 153 Additional Note – Justice Sardar Ejaz Ishaq Khan I had the pleasure of reading the judgment authored by my learned brother. I derive even greater pleasure in agreeing with its lucid analysis and conclusions. His herculean effort in synthesizing diverse and conflicting precedent over the rather diffuse topic of tampered vehicles merits recognition with a deliberate and sustained implementation by all State authorities. 2 The impetus for this additional note came from my learned brother‘s dive into the conceptual foundations for the protection of property rights, which brought up quotations from the political philosophy of John Locke and jurisprudential commentaries by later Western academics. I thought I would add this additional note to highlight that the doctrinal bedrock for the sanctity of private property rights against confiscatory legislative or executive measures is not beholden to the political philosophers of the Enlightenment era, but goes much prior in time to the prescriptions of monotheistic religions, the most explicit being those in the Quran. That the ‗social contract‘ between the citizen and the State must be premised on justice is such a fundamental Quranic injunction that any legislative or executive measure that enables confiscatory application would fall foul of, or to put in legal parlance, would be ‗ultra vires‘, the Divine command in the Quran in the same vein as a statute contravening the fundamental rights would be ultra vires the Constitution. The Quran commands in Surah Al-Baqarah as follows:

―And do not devour one another’s possessions wrongfully, and neither employ legal artifices with a Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 154 view to devouring sinfully, and knowingly, anything that by right belongs to others.‖ (2:188)

3 Our jurisprudence is rife with judgments by our Superior Courts drawing enlightenment and guidance from Islamic injunctions to render their judgments or to strike down confiscatory legislation or executive measures in numerous spheres, including land reforms , matrimony , inheritance , and gifts . Articles 2A and 227 of the Constitution provide the basis for such integration. A full bench of the Supreme Court has held that, faced with competing interpretations of law, the one closer to Islamic injunctions should be followed .

4 The instant judgment will be an addition to that list in subjecting the reading and application of section 187-A of the Customs Act to the qualifications and conditions enumerated in the main judgment. Bypassing those qualifications and conditions will render section 187-A a ‗sinful legal artifice‘ on the touchstone of the Quranic verse cited above, for it will deprive innocent citizens of their vehicles by exercising civil forfeiture without fault-based culpability judged after due process, based on best evidence of preserved integrity through proper custody and transmission.

5 The discussion in the main judgment over the primacy of the private property rights and the imperative towards the use of the least restrictive measures proportionate to the objective sought to be achieved, and the principle of fault-based forfeiture, Translation: Muhammad Asad Qazalbash Waqf vs Chief Land Commissioner, PLD 1990 SC 99 Ambreen Akram vs Asadullah Khan, 2026 SCMR 1 Abrar Hussain vs Mst. Shahida and others, PLD 2026 SC 42 Tanvir Sarfraz Khan vs Federation of Pakistan 2025 SCMR 98 Hamza Rasheed Khan vs Election Appellate Tribunal, PLD 2024 SC 1028 Custom Reference No. 12 of 2022 P a g e | 155 are all findings that fall squarely within the ambit of Islamic injunctions.

6 Therefore, the question of law relating to the scope and validity of section 187-A of the Customs Act is answered that instances of application of section 187-A sans the conditions and qualifications recorded in the main judgment would suffer from operational invalidity by contravening Articles 2A and 227 of the Constitution (in addition to other Articles of the Constitution noted in the main judgment).
